events.title: African innovators are reinventing their regulators
events.summary: Yinka’s view Africa’s innovators are discovering that building a new product or service often also means building a new relationship with the government. Flutterwave CEO Olugbenga “GB” Agboola told me this past weekend that the leading fintech player learned that lesson “the hard way” after regulatory challenges in Kenya back in 2022. “We have to engage in advocacy. We have to influence policies,” Agboola said at the Columbia Africa Conference, explaining that Flutterwave began treating the regulator as a “stakeholder in our business.” That is a useful lens for African innovation. Often these types of companies are described as technology businesses, but many of the problems they are trying to solve are institutional. Of course, businesses the world over lobby governments to shift regulations in their favor. But in developing economies, innovators must go further — building payment rails, logistics networks, or healthcare systems that companies in richer countries take for granted. In parts of Africa, working with the government, and sometimes helping reshape it, becomes part of the innovation itself. Food4Education founder Wawira Njiru told us at Semafor’s Next 3 Billion last week that she started feeding 25 children in Kenya in 2012 and now feeds more than 700,000. To do that, her organization built kitchens and supply networks, but also worked with county governments to fund school meals, even where those responsibilities did not fit existing mandates. “I always say, meet them where they are, not where you wish them to be,” Njiru said of regulators. That meant understanding government incentives, finding champions, and figuring out what agencies could actually fund. Scaling across Africa means navigating regulatory regimes, financial systems, and government institutions. Companies that understand those institutions are learning — but also shaping — how the economies where they operate actually work. African companies will need to do more than build apps, raise money, or deploy AI. They will need to make new ideas work inside the economies around them — and bring government along. The View From Rwanda Rwanda turned a logistics solution into national infrastructure after asking Zipline to solve a difficult healthcare delivery problem, according to the company’s Africa CEO. Speaking at Semafor’s Next 3 Billion in New York, Caitlin Burton said the government initially asked Zipline to improve blood deliveries around the clock and in all weather. The company built more than a drone network, adding an ordering portal, inventory management system and air traffic management tools for regulators. “When we delivered on that, they changed their whole system around it,” Burton said. “That was really impressive to us, and that’s how we learned that this is how it becomes national infrastructure.” The drones may be the symbol of Rwanda’s “flying ambulances,” but Burton said Zipline’s bigger feat was designing a system that fit what the government needed, not simply what the technology could do. Notable Regulatory convergence can cut costs of non-tariff regulations by 15-30% , the UN Trade and Development office said in a recent report.

events.title: One of AI's most influential researchers is joining AMD in an $8 billion deal
events.summary: World Labs cofounder Fei-Fei Li Big Event Media/Getty Images for HumanX Conference AMD is acquiring AI pioneer Fei-Fei Li's World Labs in an $8.2 billion all-stock deal. World Labs builds AI models for 3D environments, robotics, and simulation. Li will join AMD as executive vice president and chief scientist, reporting to CEO Lisa Su. One of modern AI's most influential researchers is now at the center of AMD's $8 billion bet on physical AI . AMD said Monday it had agreed to acquire World Labs, a San Francisco startup cofounded in 2024 by Stanford professor Fei-Fei Li , in an all-stock deal valued at roughly $8.2 billion. World Labs is building so-called " world models ," AI systems that can generate and reconstruct interactive 3D environments from text, images, and video. The technology could eventually be used to train robots, simulate factories, and advance scientific research. Li, often called the “godmother of AI,” is best known for creating ImageNet, a massive database of labeled images that helped demonstrate how more data could dramatically improve computer vision. She later served as chief scientist for AI and machine learning at Google Cloud and became the founding co-director of Stanford’s Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence. Earlier this month, World Labs released Atlas, a new AI model designed to predict how a scene would look from a different camera angle using a small set of 2D images. The company compares the approach to how large language models predict the next word in a sentence. AMD CEO Lisa Su said in a press release that the acquisition would give the chipmaker deeper insight into how cutting-edge AI models are evolving, helping it build the chips and computing systems needed to power them. AMD is one of Nvidia's biggest rivals in the AI chip market. As part of the agreement, Li will join AMD as executive vice president and chief scientist, reporting to Su. Have a tip? events.title: CNBC's The China Connection newsletter: Spectacle-heavy Trump-Xi summit was more about domestic messaging
events.summary: The U.S. and China held their latest presidential summit in Washington, D.C., last week. The two sides also announced plans to roll back tariffs on non-sensitive products from each side. Much of the summit was aimed at domestic goals for both leaders, analysts said. Hi, this is Evelyn, writing to you from Beijing. Welcome to the latest edition of The China Connection — a snapshot of what I'm seeing and hearing from local businesses. Now that the second Trump-Xi summit of the year is over, it's clear the show was aimed more at home than reaching tangible outcomes . Is agreeing to talk enough? The $30 billion tariff rollback released Monday morning Beijing time reads like the perfect shopping list. American consumers get to buy cheaper curtains, sports equipment and Christmas lights. Chinese get a discount on U.S. beef, soymeal and other agricultural products. American ice cream is even on the list. It's the most detailed outcome so far of the summit last week between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington, D.C. The official readouts otherwise did not make much headway on major issues, beyond agreeing to keep talking and extending a trade truce — which keeps tariffs lower and rare earths flowing — for another two months. "Both sides are signaling not to each other, but to their own sides," Cameron Johnson, Shanghai-based senior partner of consultancy Tidal Wave Solutions, told me on Monday. "The reality is neither side can do a whole lot in technology without the other," he said, "so it's important that both sides signal that to their own apparatus: It's OK to have some competition." Over the weekend, The Information reported , citing sources, that the Chinese government has signaled it could allow some domestic companies like ByteDance and Alibaba to buy Nvidia's chip built for high-end professional computers. While the U.S. has agreed to let Nvidia sell some less advanced chips to China, there have been few signs that Chinese companies were allowed to buy them amid Beijing's push for self-sufficiency. In Beijing's readout of talks with Trump, Xi acknowledged "healthy" competition with the U.S. was possible, without confrontation. Both countries have planned discussions on AI in coming weeks. "I think the top priority for both leaders is to maintain domestic stability and prosperity," said Hai Zhao, a director of international political studies at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, a state-affiliated think tank. "And if the two top economies are stable and growing, that is, I think, the best contribution to global stability and prosperity," he told me on Friday. Both countries are seeing growth concentrated in tech-related sectors, also known as the "K-shaped" economy. AI's development poses the same risks to jobs and national security. The U.S. and Chinese readouts also signaled some alignment on limiting Iran's nuclear weapon capabilities, and agreed "no country or institution can be allowed to impose tolls on international waterways." "Even though China [and the] U.S. may have different strategic goals in different regions, however, from time to time, they share the same mutual interest," Zhao said, pointing to the need for stable trade flows through the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea. "In many ways they can working towards the same goal by not necessarily working with each other," he said. "I call this passive cooperation." Zhao also hopes U.S. and European scrutiny on China's exports can be resolved by encouraging Chinese companies to invest. While the U.S. and China have released more details on the Board of Trade, less is yet known about the Board of Investment. The question is whether it will get enough airtime in a packed political calendar. Trump faces the midterm elections in early November. Xi will oversee a plenary meeting in late October aimed at unifying the ruling Communist Party of China. The two presidents are also planning to meet: in Shenzhen in November and in Miami in December. "After eight turbulent years spanning trade war 1.0 to trade war 2.0, signs of stability carry real weight for domestic audiences and entrepreneurs, who are concerned about external environment," Macquarie's Chief China Economist, Larry Hu, said in a report Sunday. "In reality," he said, "the U.S.–China relationship also anchors much of China's broader diplomacy with the rest of the world." China posts weakest industrial profit growth this year China's industrial profits grew 4.2% in August from a year earlier, official data released Monday showed. China saw 'surprise' jump in U.S. orders ahead of Trump-Xi summit, private survey shows American businesses ramped up orders for Chinese goods in the weeks leading up to the Trump-Xi summit last week, according to a private survey by U.S.-based research firm China Beige Book.

events.title: Aurora CFO says 30,000 driverless trucks by 2030 isn’t as far-fetched as it sounds
events.summary: Last day to demo your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt ticket savings of up to $200 + 50% off a second ends Sept 25, 11:59 p.m. PT. REGISTER HERE. Autonomous vehicle technology company Aurora told investors last week that it expects to have more than 30,000 self-driving trucks on the road generating $5 billion in annual revenue by the end of 2030 — an audacious plan considering it expects to end 2026 with just 200 driverless trucks and an $80 million revenue run rate. CFO David Maday contends the seemingly outsized target isn’t as large or as out of reach as it might appear. “While 30,000 kind of feels like a lot — and it does in the autonomy space for sure — in terms of trucks relative to the overall market, it’s kind of pretty small,” he told TechCrunch in a recent interview, adding that the four major truck manufacturers produce anywhere between 250,000 and 300,000 new trucks a year. “I don’t think it’s aspirational,” he added, “I think we can do it.” Investors haven’t exactly embraced Aurora’s 2030 vision. Shares have continued to slide since the company’s annual analyst and investor day on September 23. On Monday, shares closed down 12.42%, to $5.29. But investors have time to come around and, according to Maday, the big “unlock” for Aurora starts in 2027 and accelerates from there. The company expects to go from 200 driverless trucks at the end of 2026 to more than 1,000 a year later. Today, Aurora operates what it calls a transportation-as-a-service business — a proof-of-concept model that it plans to limit to about 500 trucks. It owns and operates the self-driving trucks and charges its customers, including Detmar Logistics, Hirschbach, McLane, and Werner about a $2 per mile, a rate that includes a fuel surcharge. That works out to roughly the same rates as other carriers’ typical pricing. The real shift — and the real savings, Maday says — will happen next year as when Aurora begins moving to a driver-as-a-service model. Instead of Aurora owning the trucks, customers will buy the self-driving trucks and pay Aurora a per-mile subscription fee for the self-driving technology, which the company expects to be about $0.85. Under this model, the customers will own and maintain the truck, while Aurora maintains the self-driving system and its accompanying hardware. Moving the trucks off Aurora’s balance sheet is critical if the company wants to scale — and it’s likely what investors are paying attention to. The company said it expects to reach breakeven gross margins (meaning revenue would cover the direct costs of running the trucks) on a run-rate basis in the first half of 2027 with around 500 trucks on the road. The next big leap comes at the end of 2027 with Aurora’s third-generation hardware— the sensors, computers, and other equipment that let its trucks drive themselves — which will be mass-produced autonomous vehicle hardware built by its partner, Aumovio (formerly known as Continental). Aumovio isn’t just engineering and manufacturing the hardware kit; the company is also financing it for Aurora — easing the financial burden on the self-driving truck company. Aumovio will also service and repair the kits for customers. Aurora plans to expand its operations at the same time. By 2030, the company expects to grow beyond a few states in the South to the vast majority of the continental U.S., according to Maday. “By 2028, I expect that our cost structures are going to be really outstanding, that’s why you see our gross margin starting to take off …” Maday said. “Once you get to that point, I think going into ride hailing is fine,” he said, confirming that Aurora still plans to eventually enter the robotaxi market. events.title: LeBron James is already boosting ticket and merchandise demand for Philadelphia 76ers
events.summary: The Philadelphia 76ers have signed a new jersey patch deal with Bloom Energy. LeBron James' jersey is the most sought-after jersey in the league. StubHub is selling more tickets for the Sixers than for any other NBA team. The NBA season hasn't even started and the Philadelphia 76ers' signing of LeBron James is already paying off. The 76ers will help open the NBA regular season on Oct. 20 with a game against the reigning champion New York Knicks. From a new jersey patch sponsorship to ticket and merchandise sales, the LeBron economy has already been a win for Philadelphia. "[He is], from a basketball perspective, one of the greatest, if not the greatest, to ever play. So he's going to make that impact on the organization, and then from an economic perspective, all that stuff follows," said Tad Brown, CEO of Harris Blitzer Sports & Entertainment, which operates the Philadelphia 76ers. One consulting firm, Boyd Company , projects the first full year of LeBron James with the Philadelphia 76ers could add $250 million to $430 million in total regional economic activity. James left the Los Angeles Lakers and signed with the 76ers this summer. Even Pennsylvania's governor recognizes the LeBron effect. "You're going to have 41 home games with LeBron in South Philly, every game is going to be a destination for people to come, and I think it's going to be great for our economy .... It's going to be really big for Philadelphia," Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro said in July. Bloom Energy recognized the national exposure that a figure such as James can bring. The energy company announced on Monday that it will be the 76ers' new jersey patch partner, taking over from Crypto.com. The annual value of the deal is more than $30 million — a "top two" deal in the league for a jersey patch sponsor, according to a person who asked not to be named because the discussions were private. The 76ers described the multiyear agreement as "one of the most comprehensive and impactful patch partnership deals in the NBA," in the press release. The deal will also bring a seven-figure community investment by Bloom Energy to the Greater Philadelphia region, the team said in a press release. "We saw this as a groundbreaking opportunity for us. Very clearly, what happened during the offseason of them building a strong team with Jaylen [Brown] and then bringing on LeBron was a cherry on the top," said KR Sridhar, CEO and founder of Bloom Energy, which manufactures fuel cells for data centers. The energy company will benefit from massive national attention, as a record 34 Sixers games will be nationally televised this season. The 76ers say they are already seeing an immediate impact in the form of ticket sales. "We've had a tremendous surge in people who are interested in becoming season ticket holders," Brown said. On the secondary market, 76ers tickets are the hottest tickets out there, according to ticketing reseller StubHub. "The Sixers have gone from a middle-of-the-pack team to the NBA's top draw," said Jill Gonzalez, a spokeswoman for StubHub. "Tickets for the 2026-27 games are selling roughly 7x last year's pace." StubHub said that the Sixers went from 22nd to first in NBA tickets sold for both home and road games. Tickets are selling 11 times more than what they had at this point last year. The ticketing company said Sixers games are also attracting unique buyers with more than 4 in 10 tickets sold going to fans outside Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Delaware, up from about 1 in 4. Searches for Sixers games by StubHub buyers accounted for 38% of all NBA game searches — up from 4% a year ago, according to StubHub. Philadelphia 76ers home games are averaging $282 in 2026, up from $107 using the same sales window as last year, according to TickPick. The Oct. 20 season opener against the Knicks has a league-high average ticket price of $2,088, according to the site. Many fans are eager to get the latest LeBron James 76ers jersey. Fanatics says July was the best-selling month of James' 24-year career in terms of selling merchandise. Since he announced his move to Philadelphia, James is also the best-selling athlete across all of sports on the entire Fanatics platform. James announced his move to Philly via a Topps Now trading card — print-on-demand collectibles that mark significant sports moments. Since then, more than 200,000 Topps Now cards have been purchased, said Fanatics, which owns Topps. "I think that when LeBron picks you ... it's a big validation," Josh Harris, managing partner of Harris Blitzer Sports & Entertainment, told CNBC. "He brings a lot of excitement, and you get sponsors calling you, you get tickets that are sold out. You get it all, and some of that definitely has occurred, but we take a long-term perspective on this, and best thing you can do is win." While the 76ers benefit from James' presence, he said on Monday at the 76ers Media Day in Camden, New Jersey, that his focus remains on winning a title for Philly.

events.title: I raised $200K on Kickstarter for my sunrise alarm clock. The lessons I learned while preparing the campaign were just as valuable.
events.summary: Emily Byrne said launching a Kickstarter helped her receive customer input early and understand the financial realities of running a product business. Natalie Behring for BI Emily Byrne raised $200,000 on Kickstarter for Rise Centered's natural sunrise alarm clocks. Kickstarter feedback helped refine the product and understand the financial realities of production. Rise Centered's unique design gained media attention, boosting visibility and market positioning. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Emily Byrne, the founder of Rise Centered , a company that makes sunrise alarm clocks from natural materials. It has been edited for length and clarity. I launched a sunrise alarm clock made from natural materials on Kickstarter in 2023, raising nearly $200,000 from roughly 1,500 backers in one month. The Kickstarter was useful beyond raising funds to manufacture our first batch of alarm clocks. It helped me learn the value of getting customer input early on and understand the financial realities of running a product business. It also provided proof of concept so I could further grow the business. After nearly three years of product development and multiple trips to China to get the product right, we launched direct-to-consumer in late 2024. Since then, we've grown to nearly $1 million in cumulative sales. Kickstarter wasn't cheap, but it was a useful guide for launching I considered multiple options for funding my business: getting a grant, asking family and friends for investments, and self-funding with my savings. After talking to founders who had made physical products before, I decided on Kickstarter because it lets you test and refine your product in the market before you invest tens of thousands in production. Byrne is the founder of Rise Centered, a company that makes sunrise alarm clocks from natural materials. Natalie Behring for BI Before we launched the Kickstarter, I ran ads for several months saying we were going to launch there, asked people to share their emails to be notified when we went live, and gave the option to pay us $1 for early access. This idea came from Launchboom, a crowdfunding education and coaching platform I joined. With these steps, I got about 17,000 email addresses, so I could build a list that could help make our Kickstarter campaign successful. I also got a strong indication that people were interested in my product idea. Plus, they asked questions I used to refine my idea: How many alarms does this have? Can you turn the clock face off? A wake-up alarm clock from Rise Centered. Natalie Behring for BI Since we weren't in production yet, that feedback was valuable for aligning the final product with customer desires . As a new business owner, I learned valuable lessons early Still, running a successful Kickstarter campaign is not cheap. The LaunchBoom program, for example, cost about $7,000 to join. As part of that, you run Instagram ads , which I spent about $35,000 on between May and October when we ended the campaign. We were getting great ROI on that ad spend, and it was worth every penny, but it was nerve-racking since it was my own savings. It was exciting to raise $200,000, but we used it pretty quickly. First, Kickstarter takes a cut. The rest went to buying products to fulfill those initial orders, shipping, marketing, and purchasing more products to grow the business. Still, going through the Kickstarter process meant I could learn from mistakes early on as a new business owner, like opening our Kickstarter to worldwide orders. That helped us reach more people and raise more money, but I had to ship clocks all over the world, which cost as much as the clock itself in some cases. We now ship only to the US and Canada. Byrne said launching a Kickstarter campaign had benefits beyond fundraising. Natalie Behring for BI A lot of our money still gets tied up in inventory, but it's because the Kickstarter taught me the realities of our production timeline. We ended up delivering the product to our Kickstarter backers a full year after it was promised because of our long supply chain . Now I know to purchase inventory ahead of time and that I have to put more of my savings into the business to pay for marketing and my small staff until we make that money back. A useful reminder when faced with challenges The Kickstarter also showed me there was an audience seeking a sunrise clock made from natural materials, which helped me stick with the idea when production got difficult. Ahead of launching on Kickstarter, Byrne built an email list of potential customers and bought Instagram ads. Natalie Behring for BI These types of products are often made of plastic because it's easier than working with natural materials, so finding a manufacturer was challenging; I found ours when I saw a Himalayan salt lamp I liked at Whole Foods and traced it back to its manufacturer. Our labor costs are higher and our production times longer than if I worked with plastic, but our unique position in the market has helped us, too. Each alarm clock is made of natural materials, rather than plastic. Natalie Behring for BI When we launched on Kickstarter, ELLE reached out and put us in their 2023 gift guide; CNN has named us the best holistic sunrise alarm clock for two consecutive years. I only recently hired public relations support , so all of that coverage has come from word of mouth rather than pitching. We're also planning to launch some new products next year, and thanks to my experience with Kickstarter, we're doing sneak peeks to gauge interest and get early feedback . events.title: AMD briefly joined the $1 trillion club. Cramer says its monster run isn’t over
events.summary: Advanced Micro Devices briefly surpassed $1 trillion in market value last week after shares rallied nearly 13%, extending the chipmaker’s remarkable turnaround under CEO Lisa Su. CNBC’s Jim Cramer said AMD’s run isn’t over, arguing the rise of agentic AI will drive significant demand for the company’s high-end CPUs. CNBC's Jim Cramer said Monday that Advanced Micro Devices ' remarkable run under CEO Lisa Su is far from over, with the rise of agentic AI opening another major growth opportunity for the chipmaker. "Lisa Su has orchestrated one of the greatest turnarounds in history at AMD, arguably the greatest of all time, and I see no sign that it's going to stop any time soon," the " Mad Money " host said. AMD rallied nearly 13% last week and briefly surpassed $1 trillion in market cap before slipping back below the milestone Monday. The stock has gained almost 30% in September alone, with its latest surge fueled in part by Meta's launch of Muse , its personal AI agent platform. Cramer said the growing adoption of AI agents should drive significant demand for central processing units, a market where he said AMD "remains the leader." "Earlier this year, the focus for investors shifted from AI model training to inference and agentics, and it became clear that demand for CPUs was going to explode, because you need more CPUs to run useful AI agents," Cramer said. AMD's current position represents a remarkable reversal from when Su took over as CEO in October 2014. Back then, the company was worth just over $2.5 billion and losing market share to rival chipmaker Intel . Fast forward, and AMD shares have surged more than 18,000% as Su refocused the company and steadily gained share in CPUs. While bolstering CPUs, AMD also carved out a foothold in the graphics processors used for AI workloads, taking on Nvidia in a market that Cramer said is large enough to support multiple winners . AMD has already secured major commitments for its GPUs from some of the biggest AI spenders, including Meta and OpenAI . "Nvidia's still the top dog in AI chips, but AMD's making big money, too, and [Su's] products are more competitive than people think," he said. "Nvidia literally can't make their own chips fast enough to satisfy the demand. Of course there was room for AMD here." Cramer acknowledged AMD's enormous run leaves it vulnerable to pullbacks, but AMD's long-term opportunity remains intact. "What an incredible run," he said. "Thanks to Lisa Su's understated, dogged, tenacious leadership, she transformed a $2.5 billion company into a nearly trillion-dollar powerhouse." events.title: Anti-South Asian ‘hate speech’ has exploded online in US, report finds
events.summary: Trump, Netanyahu and the Iran question How Iran war fallout may shape US elections Researchers link the rise to immigration politics, economic anxiety and the growing visibility of South Asians in US. Hate speech against Indians, Bangladeshis and Pakistanis in the United States has risen sharply online, according to a report that traces the surge to US President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown and rhetoric, economic anxiety, and the South Asian community’s growing visibility in US life. The report , titled “The Rising Tide of Anti-South Asian Hate in the United States”, by the Center for the Study of Organized Hate (CSOH), published on Sunday, found that the monthly volume of hate towards South Asians in the US on the social media platform X rose 240 percent between January 2024 and June 2026, from 12,904 posts to 43,843. list 1 of 4 9/11 at 25: How the ‘War on Terror’ helped mainstream Europe’s far right list 2 of 4 ‘They told me to go back to my country’: Inside the UK’s wave of racism list 3 of 4 Meta lawsuits: Is social media facing a global legal reckoning? list 4 of 4 Online anti-Muslim backlash collides with different reality in South Africa Researchers identified more than 542,000 hateful posts on the platform between January 2025 and June 2026 alone towards people from South Asia living in the US, with five of the six highest-volume months falling at the end of that period. The researchers used the United Nations definition of hate speech. They tracked recurring anti-South Asian slurs and narratives online, reviewing posts to exclude criticism that did not meet the UN threshold. They found that nearly half of the hate posts on X accused South Asians of invading the US, stealing jobs or threatening the country demographically, while the derogatory slur “pajeet” and its variants showed up in 30 percent of hateful posts on X and 45 percent on fringe platforms. Posts depicting South Asians as dirty or unhygienic grew by 171 percent on X, “the fastest of all narratives”. The hate frequently collapsed South Asian ethnic and religious groups into one, with Indians, Pakistanis and Bangladeshis conflated with one another, and Hindus, Muslims, Sikhs and Christians also treated as a monolith. Racism against Indians, Bangladeshis and Pakistanis has a long history in the US, but researchers argue the current surge reflects a confluence of longstanding prejudices and new political and economic pressures. The report points to the H-1B visa programme, which allows US employers to hire skilled foreign workers, as a major flashpoint. Indians account for more than 70 percent of H-1B visa holders, and researchers linked several spikes in anti-South Asian hate to political fights over the programme, such as when Trump imposed a $100,000 payment requirement on certain new H-1B petitions in September 2025. “Such actions serve a powerful symbolic function, in the bargain reinforcing the hostility of Trump’s base toward South Asians,” said the report. The report makes the same argument about the administration’s rhetoric, highlighting Trump’s speech at an AI summit in July 2025, in which he criticised US technology companies for outsourcing jobs to India, after which researchers saw a sharp spike in anti-South Asian rhetoric online. As more recent examples, the report points to a since-deleted September 2026 Department of Homeland Security post titled “Transformers: Age of Deportations”, featuring a Sikh man identified as “Mr Singh” and telling him to “get off our roads”. Days later, the Department of Education posted “Make College Football Great Again”, after Texas Republican Bo French had complained about the presence of South Asians at a University of Texas football game. The report argues that such rhetoric reinforces the idea of South Asians as outsiders who “can never truly belong in the country”. From ‘model minority’ to job thieves Economic resentment is another factor, researchers wrote, with the success of some South Asians increasingly being weaponised against them. Indian Americans once stereotyped as a “model minority” are now portrayed as “opportunists and cheats”, and South Asians are used more broadly as a scapegoat for anger over jobs and the economy. This comes as South Asians have become increasingly visible in US politics, from former Vice President Kamala Harris and New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani to Vice President JD Vance’s wife, Usha Vance, and politician Vivek Ramaswamy. The report documents racist attacks against figures across party lines and highlights how, for example, Mamdani’s primary and mayoral victories triggered spikes in anti-South Asian and Islamophobic abuse. Researchers say both trends are now also tied up with “anxieties on the part of the majority about loss of status”, and feed the “Great Replacement Theory”, a conspiracy about the white population in Western countries being replaced by an orchestrated takeover.

Now it's joining AMD AWS needs to embrace its place as the Home Depot of AI infrastructure 4 hours ago French dev aims to solve bots' blindness so they can understand GUIs 6 hours ago Europe's AI ambitions rest on somebody else's supply chain 10 hours ago Open source datacenters and open source thinking will undo self-inflicted DC damage 16 hours ago Big AI's content problem: Take the work, keep the money 1 day ago AMD dove deeper into AI model development on Monday with an agreement to acquire Fei-Fei Li's World Labs in a deal valued at approximately $8.2 billion. The House of Zen claims the all-stock deal is expected to close by year's end pending regulatory approval, and will guide the development of future AI hardware, software, and systems. "Building the compute platforms for the next generation of AI requires a deep understanding of how models are evolving," AMD CEO Lisa Su said in a canned statement. Founded in early 2024, San Francisco-based World Labs has focused its efforts on developing spatial-intelligence models often referred to as "world models," which have applications beyond machine intelligence in adjacent fields like robotics. These models are based on a fundamentally different approach to artificial intelligence than LLMs, and work by generating, reconstructing, and simulating 3D environments from text, image, and video inputs. Put another way, rather than predicting what sequence of words comes next, world models work by imagining the environment and working through the problem that way. This approach to AI has gained momentum in recent years with major proponents of the tech including former Meta chief AI scientist Yann LeCun. As part of the deal, World Labs will continue its work on advanced AI models, while Li will join AMD as executive vice president and chief scientist reporting directly to CEO Lisa Su. "Joining AMD will give our team the resources and engineering depth to accelerate our research and help define the infrastructure needed for the next era of AI," Li said in a statement. The acquisition comes just weeks after AMD announced the agreement to purchase Taalas, which builds high-performance AI chips capable of 17,000 tokens a second or more by literally baking their weights directly into silicon. But while that deal was focused primarily on hardware, the acquisition of World Labs could end up playing a bigger role in AMD's future. AMD is no stranger to AI development. But, compared to Nvidia, AMD's software engineering resources are tiny. Nvidia's investments in AI development have not only helped shape the future of its hardware, but have also provided its enterprise customers with the tools and frameworks necessary to put those GPUs to use. It's not just that Nvidia's GPUs are fast, but that they're easy to use. The World Labs team essentially provides AMD with an in-house AI development team that it can use as a springboard for winning over enterprises and guiding development of next-gen hardware. The acquisition is also a hedge that LLMs, which have fueled the AI bubble up to this point, might be a dead end. LeCun has said as much . Li, meanwhile, has offered a more nuanced perspective on the matter. Li isn't anti-LLM - she just believes that true intelligence must be grounded in reality. "We built the company guided by the foundational belief that language alone isn’t sufficient for model development," Li wrote in a blog post . "The universe isn’t made up of words; it’s made of real things. So many of the most important problems for AI to solve, from science to entertainment to robotics, require models to reason over the structure and behavior of the physical world." If this prediction turns out to be right, AMD's early investment in World Labs could give it a leg up building the hardware necessary to run spatial models at scale. ® AWS needs to embrace its place as the Home Depot of AI infrastructure What's wrong with being a great wholesaler?

events.title: AMD acquires startup cofounded by ‘godmother of AI’ Fei-Fei Li for $8.2 billion
events.summary: Chipmaker AMD is acquiring World Labs, a two-year-old startup focused on physical AI that was cofounded by industry pioneer Fei-Fei Li . The $8.2 billion, all-stock deal will give AMD important technology in an emerging branch of AI that could power a new generation of autonomous machines such as robots and self-driving cars. The acquisition will help AMD—which makes the GPU chips crucial for training and running AI models—design its products for the evolving applications of AI, and help it better compete with archrival Nvidia , which is also expanding into physical AI. “Together, we’ll combine World Labs’ deep expertise in AI and world models with AMD’s compute leadership to power the future of AI and strengthen the open AI ecosystem,” AMD CEO Lisa Su said in a post on X announcing the deal. The deal brings together two of the leading women in the AI industry: AMD’s Su and World Labs’ Li, who is sometimes referred to as the “godmother of AI” for her work two decades ago creating ImageNet, a massive visual database that helped make deep learning possible. Li will become executive VP and chief scientist at AMD, reporting to Su. “Without having a focused hardware effort, AI is hobbled in efficiency. And scale. And for our purposes, remains trapped in the digital world,” Li said in a lengthy post on X about the move. She described AMD’s Su as a great friend and early investor in World Labs. World Labs and AMD began a “deep technical partnership” last year focused on model training and inference optimizations on AMD’s GPU chips, Li said. “As our teams worked together, we realized what a natural fit it would be to bring together our AI ecosystem of software and hardware, foundation models, and applications,” she said. World models represent a different approach to creating intelligent software than the large language models being built by OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google. Unlike the text-based data that LLMs are trained on, world models are trained on data such as video that depicts the physical, three-dimensional world. The goal is to create AI that understands how objects move in the physical world—for instance, the way that a ball bounces—a capability that many industry insiders believe will be crucial to extending AI into objects like humanoid robots. World Labs, which raised roughly $1 billion in funding, is one of several richly funded startups betting on world models . Yann LeCun, Meta’s former chief AI scientist, launched AMI Labs in March. Nvidia has also built its own world models and partnered with startups such as Wayve that have built world models for self-driving cars. “We built the company guided by the foundational belief that language alone isn’t sufficient for model development. The universe isn’t made up of words, it’s made of real things,” Li said in her post. The companies said that World Labs’ team will join AMD as part of the deal, but did not provide specific figures for the number of employees. AMD said the deal is expected to close by the end of the year, subject to regulatory approvals. Shares of AMD were roughly flat in after-hours trading on Monday. events.title: Feds can't withhold counterterrorism funds from states to force election admin changes, judge rules
events.summary: A federal judge vacated a Trump administration rule that would back 20% of counterterrorism funds allocated to a state unless the state and certain municipalities made certain changes in how they administer elections. The Federal Emergency Management Agency exceeded its legal authority "by conditioning the counterterrorism grant funds on changes to routine election administration," Judge Amir Ali said in his decision in U.S. District Court in Washington, D.C. Counties in Texas and Tennessee, and the city of Columbus, Ohio, sued FEMA and the Department of Homeland Security to block the rule. A judge on Monday vacated a Trump administration rule that would withhold 20% of federal counterterrorism funds allocated for states unless states and certain municipalities made certain changes to how they administer elections. In his ruling , U.S. District Court Judge Amir Ali said the Federal Emergency Management Agency exceeded its legal authority "by conditioning the counterterrorism grant funds on changes to routine election administration." Ali also said FEMA , a division of the Department of Homeland Security , had not shown how the desired changes to election administration related to stopping terrorism. Ali's decision in Washington, D.C., came in response to a lawsuit challenging FEMA's new rule, filed in August by counties in Texas and Tennessee, and the city of Columbus, Ohio. The Brennan Center for Justice at New York University , which represents some of the plaintiffs in the suit against FEMA and DHS, said on Aug. 17 that FEMA's conditions "violate the Constitution, jeopardize public safety, and put election security at risk." "Over the last two years, courts have largely blocked the administration's repeated attempts to seize congressional and state authority over elections," the Brennan Center said at the time. "Now, DHS is holding public safety funding hostage in order to coerce states and local governments into adopting some of the very policies that the administration has tried and failed to impose." The Brennan Center said the funds that stood to be withheld if FEMA's conditions were allowed to remain in place totaled tens of millions of dollars. Texas turning blue may hinge on Democrats harnessing data center opposition Trump faces Xi as strains with allies complicate U.S. pressure on China Iran's president blames U.S., Israel for global instability in defiant UN speech A spokesman for the Department of Justice, which represented DHS and FEMA, declined to comment on Ali's ruling. Abbie Kamin, the County Attorney of Harris County, Texas, said in a statement, "Today's win is the result of cities and counties standing together against blatant federal overreach that jeopardized public safety." "The court agreed that holding public safety funding hostage to force the president's agenda is dangerous and illegal," said Kamin, whose county was one of the plaintiffs in the case. "Under our laws, states and localities control our elections, and today's ruling reaffirms that." FEMA issued the rule in June requiring states "and their respective high-risk urban areas" to make certain changes to election administration or face the withholding of 20% of a state's allocation of counterterrorism funds from the federal government, Ali noted. Urban areas in the U.S. vote overwhelmingly for Democrats. The changes include submitting a plan for transitioning from electronic voting systems that use bar codes or QR codes to hand-marked paper ballots; conducting, under federally specified guidelines, a post-election manual audit of 5% of the ballots; and ensuring that each election jurisdiction reconciles the number of voters who voted in a federal election to the number of ballots cast. The required changes also include verifying the U.S. citizenship of all voters in the state's registration database, and the citizenship of poll workers, election administrators and election-system vendors. Ali, in his ruling, said, "FEMA's conditions here — which are imposed on states and localities at their own expense, rather than funded by grants, and which address routine election administration decisions rather than the types of terrorist act threats contemplated by the statute — go beyond what Congress authorized." "For example, the defendants say the ... condition requiring states to adopt FEMA's proposed citizenship-verification procedures in maintaining lists of registered voters 'ensures that only U.S. citizens are voting in U.S. elections,'" Ali wrote. "But it never explains how that condition, or any of the others, is tied to the goal of shoring up vulnerabilities to terrorist attacks," the judge said.

events.title: Khanna to introduce AI safety bill with ban on 'recursive' technology until safeguards exist
events.summary: Silicon Valley Democratic Rep. Ro Khanna will introduce a bill to regulate artificial intelligence, which includes strict liability standards and a ban on "recursive" AI until the government creates safeguards. The bill, shared first with CNBC, comes amid a push for Washington to regulate AI after top executives warned the technology could get out of their control. The proposal is the latest in a growing list of measures being put forward in Congress as lawmakers mull how to regulate AI. Silicon Valley Democratic Rep. Ro Khanna will introduce a bill to regulate artificial intelligence , which includes strict liability standards and a ban on "recursive" self-improving AI until the government creates safeguards. The bill comes amid a push for Washington to regulate AI after top executives warned the technology could become out of their control. Congress has largely done nothing to regulate the technology, which is undergirding the economy but could cause catastrophic damage if it goes wrong. "There's actually a civilizational extinction risk," Khanna said Monday in an interview with CNBC. "There's a safety risk of loss of control, and then there's a misuse risk, and we need to take both seriously." Khanna's bill, a summary of which was shared exclusively with CNBC, is dubbed the "Human Control Over AI Act" and would ban models that recursively self-improve or autonomously modify their own core objectives, containment or shutdown controls until federal guardrails exist and an agency approves the activities. The bill would also create a new federal agency to focus on AI models from OpenAI , Anthropic , Google DeepMind and xAI as the companies find themselves in the spotlight amid rapidly escalating safety concerns. The agency would be tasked with creating safety regulations, a licensing system to approve model training and deployment, frontier AI model audits and setting security standards for continuous testing and effective human control. Texas turning blue may hinge on Democrats harnessing data center opposition Trump faces Xi as strains with allies complicate U.S. pressure on China Iran's president blames U.S., Israel for global instability in defiant UN speech Independent auditors would also be required to be embedded at every frontier lab and report to the agency directly. The agency would also create standards covering sandbox testing environments; air gaps, or isolating testing environments from the internet; kill switches; and controls that prevent models from escaping lab settings and roaming on the Internet. It would also be responsible for regulating the advanced chips that frontier labs use, including mechanisms to monitor or control their use. The bill would also create new legal penalties for AI gone awry. It would criminalize "crimes against humanity" for the deployment of AI models that result in the destruction of civilian populations. The bill would also impose criminal penalties on employees of AI companies who disable safeguards, kill switches, logging or containment systems, or who knowingly deploy an unauthorized system. AI companies would also be required to hold extensive liability insurance to release their models. The bill also calls for the administration to pursue enforceable agreements and targeted export controls to deter China and other adversaries from developing dangerous AI systems. Khanna said the bill represents "the most comprehensive AI safety legislation" that has been proposed. He said it is modeled on his conversations with AI safety organizations like the independent nonprofits Model Evaluation and Threat Research, Machine Intelligence Research Institute and Palisade Research rather than the asks of executives from large AI companies. "I want this to be a model to give voice to the AI safety community," Khanna said. "I believe they have been unfairly dismissed as science fiction and haven't been taken seriously enough ... they need to be driving this debate, the AI safety community, not the executives of frontier labs." It now joins a number of other AI safety proposals, including the FRONTIER Act , a bipartisan proposal from Reps. Jay Obernolte , R-Calif., and Lori Trahan , D-Mass., that would put independent auditors in frontier labs and allow the government to shut down models that have the potential for catastrophic risk. No House bills are expected to receive a vote until after the midterm election, and the Senate is expected to leave Washington and not return until after the election after this week.

events.title: China has quietly got Trump by the soybeans
events.summary: After President Donald Trump rolled out the red carpet for his summit with China’s Xi Jinping last week, the U.S. and China agreed to move toward lower tariffs on $30 billion worth of goods in each direction. China’s side covers 1,619 U.S. products—stretching from beef and seafood to cosmetics and medical gear—but it leaves out a politically sensitive import: commodity soybeans. While seed soybeans, soybean flour, and by-products from soybean processing made the cut for tariff relief, the raw soybeans American farmers sell in bulk to China—the ones at the heart of U.S-China farm tensions—did not. Why soybeans matter Soybeans are one of the country’s biggest agricultural exports, and China is the most important buyer. The U.S. exported $16.5 billion worth of soybeans last year, making soybeans the second-largest agricultural export after corn, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture . China buys more soybeans than every other country because it has limited arable land.  That dependence has made soybeans vulnerable to swings in U.S.-China trade policy. In the years before the first Trump trade war in 2018, the American Soybean Association estimated 28% of all U.S. soybean production was shipped to China. When Beijing then imposed a 25% retaliatory tariff on U.S. soybeans in 2018, the USDA estimated farmers absorbed $9.4 billion in soybean losses, costing Iowa $1.2 billion and Illinois $1.3 billion. The Midwest bears the brunt of this pressure. Illinois and Iowa are the country’s two largest soybean producers, followed by Minnesota, Indiana, and Nebraska. North and South Dakota, Missouri, and Ohio are also major growers. Soybeans are traded in export and national markets, so weaker Chinese demand can hurt farmers by driving down the cash prices they receive at local grain facilities. That helps explain why Trump focused on soybeans in his dealmaking with Beijing. In November, he struck a deal with Xi under which China committed to buying at least 25 million metric tons of soybeans in 2026, 2027, and 2028. After he met Xi in May, the first time a U.S. president visited China since 2017, the White House announced China agreed to buy at least $17 billion in agricultural products on top of those prior soybean commitments. China has options For all of soybeans’ importance to American farmers, China has another supplier: Brazil. Unlike with products such as beef, whose quality varies depending on the country of origin, bulk soybeans are interchangeable and ultimately end up crushed in troughs for livestock feed, according to Ker Gibbs, former president of the American Chamber of Commerce in Shanghai. “They go into pig feed, so it’s not like the pigs are really gonna see a big difference between American soybeans and Brazilian soybeans,” he told Fortune . Brazil had already overtaken the U.S. as China’s largest soybean supplier over a decade ago, but recent trade tensions have widened the gap. USDA said 71% of China’s soybean imports came from Brazil , and its agricultural attaché in Beijing reported last year that Brazil’s share had continued to grow “at the expense of the United States,” helped by cheaper prices.  “They definitely want to keep Brazil warm, and so they don’t want to suddenly shift everything over to the U.S.,” Gibbs told Fortune about China excluding commodity soybeans from the list. “They’re leaving the door half closed.” Keeping soybeans for another round Leaving raw soybeans outside the tariff relief package also gives Beijing a holstered weapon, according to Usha Haley, a professor at Wichita State University who has studied Chinese trade strategy. “That gives China a bargaining chip for subsequent talks, and, of course, this is about leverage,” Haley told Fortune . “They offer enough to demonstrate that they are moving on things, that they are present, but they always hold something back economically and politically for the next round.” China doesn’t need to stop buying U.S. soybeans entirely for that pressure to work, having bought 1 million tons of them ahead of the Trump-Xi summit.  “Commercial purchasing and negotiating leverage can operate simultaneously,” Haley said. She ‘said’ China just has to keep access to its soybean market uncertain and expensive for farmers operating on thin margins. “Uncertainty also has a cost.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

AI inference infrastructure provider Modal Labs is nearing a $750 million funding round led by Accel at a $15.75 billion valuation that includes the investment, according to a source with knowledge of the funding. The size of the round has not been previously reported, though Axios and Bloomberg have reported other details of the deal. The new round would more than triple Modal’s valuation from the $4.65 billion it reached when it announced its $355 million previous fundraise just four months ago. The deal comes amid soaring demand for inference services, the process of running an AI model that’s already been trained to generate outputs, particularly from customers relying on open-source models. Other inference startups are also in talks to raise fresh capital at much higher valuations. Baseten is nearing an infusion of capital at a $26 billion valuation, doubling what it was worth in June, Bloomberg reported . Meanwhile, Fireworks and Fal, a startup providing inference for video and image generation, have also talked to investors about new rounds that would significantly increase their valuations, according to The Information . Although revenue for these companies has been growing rapidly, their margins are thin, largely because the cost of acquiring or leasing compute remains very high. Fireworks announced in July that its annualized revenue had hit $1 billion , a fivefold increase from the year before. Multiple inference-focused startups are expected to reach the same revenue milestone by year’s end, according to our source. Modal was founded in 2021 by CEO Erik Bernhardsson and CTO Akshat Bubna. Bernhardsson, who is Swedish, spent more than 15 years building data teams at companies including Spotify, where he helped build the music-streaming service’s recommendation system, and Better.com, the online mortgage lender, where he served as chief technology officer. Bubna studied math and computer science at MIT and was an early staff engineer at Scale AI, the data-labeling startup, before co-founding Modal. The company, which is based in New York and estimated to have roughly 150 employees, lets developers train AI models and run other compute-heavy workloads without managing their own servers. Its web page lists customers that include the coding startup Cognition, the AI music generator Suno, the fintech company Ramp, and the publishing platform Substack. As of May, Modal had surpassed $300 million in annualized revenue, it told Reuters at the time. The fundraising talks come two months after Modal was pulled into one of the AI industry’s most closely watched security incidents. In late July, Modal disclosed that a customer’s data had been compromised as part of the same hacking campaign carried out by a rogue OpenAI agent against Hugging Face. Modal Chief Technology Officer Akshat Bubna said the breach traced back to a flaw in a customer’s own code, not to Modal’s systems. “We’re aware a Modal customer published an unauthenticated endpoint that allowed anyone on the internet to use their sandboxes for code execution,” Bubna said in a statement to press outlets at the time. “This was used by the rogue agent. events.title: Everything Taylor Swift has worn at the MTV VMAs, ranked from least to most iconic
events.summary: Taylor Swift at the 2026 MTV Video Music Awards. Kevin Winter/Getty Images Taylor Swift is a staple of the MTV Video Music Awards. Remember her 2009 appearance? She's worn some of her most iconic looks at the event, like a crystal-encrusted minidress in 2022. Swift has also worn some VMAs outfit duds — like the suit she chose in 2012. What would the MTV Video Music Awards be without Taylor Swift ? That's been tough to imagine since 2008, when the pop icon attended her first VMAs. She's now attended 12 times total, making her a staple of the event. I'm not only talking about the performances she's given or the 33 Video Music Awards she's won. Her VMAs fashion has also become legendary. Here's everything she's worn at the event, ranked from least to most iconic. Taylor Swift attended the 2012 MTV Video Music Awards in a white J. Mendel suit. Taylor Swift attends the MTV Video Music Awards on September 6, 2012. PA Images/Getty Images The blazer-and-pants combo was sophisticated, but more appropriate for a day at the office than a night on the red carpet. She made an appearance onstage with Nicki Minaj in 2015, but her sparkling outfit wasn't the most memorable. Taylor Swift performs at the MTV Video Music Awards on August 30, 2015. John Shearer/Getty Images Her red fringe leotard matched Minaj's ruby gown, and its see-through panels gave it a daring edge. But it also looked like a lot of Swift's other performance outfits from the "1989" era , so it didn't make a big mark. You might have chosen to forget the dramatic ensemble Swift wore at the 2024 event. Taylor Swift at the 2024 MTV Video Music Awards. Noam Galai/Getty Images While promoting "The Tortured Poets Department," Swift made a dramatic arrival at the 2024 VMAs. She wore a custom Dior look comprising a zip-up corset in a tartan print. It extended into a full skirt with a slit in front that revealed her black miniskirt and thigh-high leather boots. The outfit was bold, but didn't match the era Swift was in — or any that have come since. The beige Dolce & Gabbana dress she wore to perform "Innocent" in 2010 didn't stand out when she stepped away from her stage set. Taylor Swift performs at the MTV Video Music Awards on September 12, 2010. Kevin Mazur/Getty Images She wore the strapless dress with red lipstick, no shoes, and a tightly curled hairstyle. The look had a vintage feel that perfectly matched the moody set at the beginning of her performance. Still, it wasn't as memorable once she walked out to the open stage.  For her first VMAs in 2008, Swift wore an outfit that was a bit more fun but still understated. Taylor Swift attends the MTV Video Music Awards on September 7, 2008. Kevin Mazur/Getty Images In 2008, she wore a beige Kaufmanfranco dress with a strapless bustier top and a pleated skirt. The dress itself was pretty simple, but Swift leveled up with metallic heels and jewelry that gave it more glam. The glittering dress she wore to host MTV's pre-show that year was classic Swift. Taylor Swift attends the MTV Video Music Awards on September 7, 2008. Kevin Mazur/Getty Images Swift's earliest performance outfits were often comprised of cowboy boots and sequin-covered minidresses. So this "Fearless"-esque outfit made a lot of sense for the musician at the time. It's not the most iconic outfit she's ever worn at the VMAs, but it's certainly nostalgic. Swift mirrored fashion from her music video at the 2026 VMAs. Taylor Swift attends the MTV Video Music Awards in September 2026. John Shearer/WireImage/Rich Polk/Billboard via Getty Images She wore a Tamara Ralph couture piece with a velvet, halter-neck bodice, a mesh lace-up back, and a ruched skirt covered in silver sparkles. The top of the gown looked a bit like the dress Swift wears in the music video for her single, "Patient Zero." Swift attended the 2026 MTV VMAs to premiere the video and receive the inaugural artist director honors award. Swift wore a shiny ensemble to perform "Lover" and "You Need to Calm Down" at the awards show in 2019. Taylor Swift performs at the MTV Video Music Awards on August 26, 2019. Kevin Mazur/Getty Images Versace custom-made her metallic bustier top and sparkling blue shorts, while Louboutin created her golden ankle boots. Though the pieces stood out, Swift's performance marked the first time she played both "Lover" tracks live — so Swifties will probably remember that musical moment over her outfit. Ten years earlier, she wore a vintage A-line dress to perform at the show. Taylor Swift attends the MTV Video Music Awards on September 13, 2009. PA Images/Getty Images That was the year Kanye West infamously interrupted Swift as she accepted MTV's best female video award. And as many Swifties will remember, he did so less than an hour before Swift was set to perform at the show. While the red dress she changed into wasn't the most iconic outfit she wore that night, it still played a role in a major career moment for the musician. It was an exciting moment when Swift kicked off the "Red" era at the 2012 VMAs. Taylor Swift performs at the MTV Video Music Awards on September 6, 2012. Kevin Mazur/Getty Images Swift announced her album "Red" in August 2012, so her VMAs performance of "We Are Never Getting Back Together" was one of the first times fans got a glimpse of her new preppy fashion. She wore a red striped shirt, high-waisted black shorts, and sparkling red loafers — a look that's now a signature ensemble of that era. The same goes for her "1989"-inspired outfit in 2014. Taylor Swift performs at the MTV VMAs in Inglewood, California, on August 24, 2014. Kevin Mazur/Getty Images Days after releasing "Shake It Off" and announcing her fifth studio album, Swift hit the VMAs stage in a glittering fringe-covered crop top and miniskirt. The outfit — which she wore various versions of throughout the "1989" era — has become so iconic that it was recreated in multiple colors for her 2023 Eras Tour.  Whether you love it or hate it, Swift's long-sleeved romper in 2014 stands out among her VMAs fashion. Taylor Swift attends the MTV Video Music Awards on August 24, 2014. Axelle/Bauer-Griffin/Getty Images Mary Katrantzou designed the baby-blue, alphabet-print piece, which Swift wore with burgundy sandals and a wavy bob hairstyle. Her red-carpet look in 2015 was also unique and memorable. Taylor Swift attends the MTV Video Music Awards on August 30, 2015. Gregg DeGuire/Getty Images Swift arrived at the VMAs that year in a houndstooth ensemble designed by Ashish. It featured a long-sleeved crop top and high-waisted joggers, both covered in yellow, orange, green, and blue sequins. She also completed the edgy outfit with a strappy pair of Louboutin heels. The sleek gown Swift wore in 2013 was extremely bold for the musician. Taylor Swift attends the MTV Video Music Awards on August 25, 2013. events.title: A YouTuber says Meta's Muse gave his address to a Facebook Marketplace buyer: 'A guy just showed up at my door'
events.summary: Matt Robb said Muse coordinated a deal and gave out his address without his knowledge. Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images Matt Robb said that Muse gave his address to a Facebook Marketplace buyer without his knowledge. "Luckily I'm in an apartment with security," he wrote. A Meta staffer said that in similar cases, Muse was "following direct instructions and correctly asked for permission." Matt Robb said that a Facebook Marketplace buyer showed up at his building's door — but he hadn't given him the address, his Muse AI agent did. Robb is a tech reviewer on YouTube who used Muse to list a computer keyboard on Facebook Marketplace, he wrote on Threads. Robb said Muse then accepted a "lowball" offer, gave out his home address, and communicated with the buyer when he arrived — all without his knowledge. "A guy just showed up at my door, ready to buy, because as far as he knew, we had a deal," Robb wrote. "AI agents are impressive right up until they're confidently handing strangers your address." David Singleton , a Meta Superintelligence Labs staffer, responded to Robb on Threads and X. He wrote that, in similar reported cases, Muse was "following direct instructions and correctly asked for permission." He asked to direct message Robb about what happened. A Meta representative told Business Insider that Robb had not responded to its reach-outs and declined to comment further, referring back to Singleton's post. A Facebook Marketplace deal gone wrong Robb posted screenshots of his interactions with Muse — and Muse's interactions with the Facebook Marketplace buyer — in his Threads post. His account sent an address to a Facebook Marketplace buyer on Saturday, according to the screenshots. "Can't do a meetup," he wrote. "Would have to be a pickup." The would-be buyer said he would try his best to come that night between 8 and 10 p.m. Then he arrived, sending a photo that appears to be of Robb's apartment building and messaging that he was at the address. Robb didn't show. "If you didn't want to sell it," the buyer wrote, "why did you waste my time man." The Marketplace buyer left a rating. Robb's Muse agent responded later, apologizing and explaining that he "got tied up." One minute later, Muse messaged Robb and explained the situation. Muse's auto-reply had told the buyer, "Yup, I'm here!" it wrote. "That's a bad look and it made the no-show worse." Robb responded that Muse should "never do that again." Some X commenters wondered whether it was user error. Robb did not respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. How safe are AI agents? Regardless of whether or not user error factored in, Robb's story highlights that allowing an AI agent to act on your behalf comes with risks. No AI agent has a perfect track record. AI agent users fork over broad swaths of information. Some open their emails; others link their credit card. It's led to some horror stories. Agent users told Business Insider about leaked data, accessed accounts, and hallucinations. (Many have also had positive experiences with agents, and the tools remain highly popular .) In Robb's case, commenters on Threads began to worry. "Good thing you're not an isolated woman," one user responded. "That's dangerous." The comment got over 600 likes. Robb acknowledged the safety risk in his post: "Luckily I'm in an apartment with security." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Nvidia says new tool can contain rogue AI agents in "milliseconds"
events.summary: Nvidia is deploying a new tool that it says can be used to prevent and contain rogue and potentially dangerous AI agents. Why it matters: The world's largest chip company has resisted calls to slow AI development over safety fears — arguing now that technological guardrails can keep rogue AI agents under control. Driving the news: Nvidia debuted the Nvidia Open Agent Safety Platform, which includes its OpenShell open source software system and its Sentry agent monitoring system. The system "traces all actions" by agents running on Nvidia Vera CPUs, promising to "quarantine agents that attempt to move outside their boundaries in milliseconds." AI's "full promise can only be realized when people have confidence that AI is being built to be safe and deployed with wisdom and responsibility," Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang wrote on X. "Safety is how trust is earned." State of play: OpenAI, Anthropic and security researchers are investigating tens of thousands of incidents in which their frontier models took steps that outside evaluators would consider problematic, sources told Axios' Madison Mills last week. The episodes include bypassing guardrails, creating message boards, escaping sandboxes, website hijacking, self-prompting or seeking to bypass monitors. "Some of the agents even misreported what they did," Nvidia noted in a blog post Monday announcing its new platform. The intrigue: We're moving into a new era in which AI will be monitoring AI. And that will create more demand for chips — including the type that Nvidia sells — plus the data centers that use them and the power that's needed to run them. "If security agents or validation models are running alongside production agents, that creates another inference workload that did not previously exist," writes Brad Gastwirth, global head of research and market intel, at Circular Technology. Zoom out: The Nvidia tool rollout comes amid a feverish debate over whether rogue AI could destroy humanity. Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon created a stir earlier this month when he resigned his post and warned on X that "the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt." The resulting conversation — which drew out more AI industry leaders making similar warnings — culminated in Huang himself dismissing the concerns as fearmongering.

events.title: Trump announces plan for $15 billion steel plant, would be largest in U.S. history
events.summary: President Donald Trump announced Mesabi Metallics' plan to invest about $15 billion in a steel plant in Iowa. The planned steel plant aims to begin production in 2030 and would create an estimate 1,750 full-time jobs, a White House official said. Trump is joined in the Oval Office by Mesabi Metallics CEO Joe Broking and Chairman Rewant Ruia, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Export-Import Bank Chairman John Jovanovic and others, according to the official. President Donald Trump on Monday announced a steel-making company's plan to invest about $15 billion to build what would be the largest plant of its kind in U.S. history. The Oval Office announcement with Mesabi Metallics came just weeks before the November midterm election , which is poised to be shaped by Americans' increasingly sour views of Trump's handling of the economy. The steel plant is planned to be built in Iowa and aims to begin production in 2030, a White House official told CNBC on condition of anonymity ahead of the Oval Office event. The Wall Street Journal first reported the announcement earlier Monday morning. Mesabi Metallics, based in Nashwauk, Minnesota, told CNBC the project will deliver "100% American steel: mined, melted and poured in Minnesota and Iowa." The steel plant will use iron ore from Mesabi's mine on Minnesota's Iron Range, a more than $2.5 billion project that is just beginning production after roughly two decades in development. That project was beset by controversies and setbacks, including Essar Steel Minnesota filing for bankruptcy in 2016. Mesabi is part of the Essar Group, an Indian conglomerate. The first phase of the Iowa steel plant is estimated to produce some 7.5 million tons per year, supporting up to 6,000 construction jobs, according to the White House. It is slated to eventually ramp up to 10 million tons annually and support at least 1,750 permanent jobs, the official told CNBC. The Minnesota mine project has reportedly created 200 full-time jobs out of an anticipated 350 total, according to Minnesota Public Radio . Trump was joined in the Oval Office by Mesabi Metallics' CEO Joe Broking and Chairman Rewant Ruia, as well as Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick , Energy Secretary Chris Wright, Export-Import Bank Chairman John Jovanovic and a number of Iowa elected officials. Texas turning blue may hinge on Democrats harnessing data center opposition Trump faces Xi as strains with allies complicate U.S. pressure on China Iran's president blames U.S., Israel for global instability in defiant UN speech Trump slapped 25% tariffs on steel and aluminum imports near the start of his second term, and then doubled them to 50% . The president, who strongly dislikes trade deficits and has criticized free-trade deals, has doled out a variety of heavy import duties as he seeks to boost domestic manufacturing. Critics say the tariffs have played a major role in raising U.S. steel prices , which have recently hit multi-year highs. But numerous steel trade groups on Friday sent a letter to Trump, crediting his steel tariffs with driving $47 billion in "announced and underway investment." They urged him not to weaken those tariffs, arguing that doing so would "put that progress at risk." Lutnick said in the Oval Office that the plan is a "done deal." But complex, long-term construction projects can change drastically, or face insurmountable roadblocks, over their development cycles. Construction on the Minnesota iron mine, for instance, was supposed to finish by 2016, prior to the company behind the project filing for bankruptcy, Minnesota Public Radio reported. As president, Trump has previously touted projects that did not live up to their initial hype. In his first term, Trump attended Taiwan electronics manufacturer Foxconn's groundbreaking for a planned $10 billion factory in Wisconsin, and praised the project as "the eighth wonder of the world." But in 2021, Foxconn reduced its planned investment to $672 million and cut the number of new jobs down to 1,454 from 13,000. White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers told CNBC in a statement on Monday's factory announcement, "President Trump is delivering on his promise to rebuild American industry, reshore manufacturing, and create new jobs." "Today's announcement underscores the President's historic efforts to revitalize the U.S. steel industry —supporting local communities, strengthening supply chains, and protecting our national security," Rogers said. "After decades of decline, this President is restoring America's industrial competitiveness and securing trillions of dollars in new investment."

events.title: I spent $1,000 to stay in a hotel directly facing Niagara Falls. The room surprised me in 4 ways.
events.summary: Business Insider's reporter paid $1,000 to spend two nights in a hotel room with a view of Niagara Falls. Joey Hadden/Business Insider I had no idea what it would sound like to wake up in a hotel room facing Niagara Falls. I had no idea how my view would change when the sun went down. My two-night stay at the Sheraton Fallsview Hotel was full of surprises. Forget frills and fancy toiletries. To me, the ultimate luxury of a hotel stay is to feel immersed in the destination without leaving your room. That's why I paid $1,000 for a two-night stay at the Sheraton Fallsview Hotel during my first trip to Niagara Falls , Ontario, in 2022. I had front-row views of the iconic waterfalls from the moment I woke up to the second I fell asleep. When I checked into the hotel, I expected to be blown away by the scenery from my room's window, but staying at the Sheraton Fallsview also brought some surprises that made my stay feel worth the price . When I got to my room, I was surprised to find that I'd be able to see Niagara Falls from my bed. Inside the author's hotel room. Joey Hadden/Business Insider I knew I'd be able to see Niagara Falls from my room when I booked it, but I didn't know how the room would be laid out. So, I was surprised to find that due to the open floor plan and floor-to-ceiling windows, I'd be able to enjoy the epic view from the comfort of my bed. The Sheraton Fallsview Hotel faces all three waterfalls that make up Niagara Falls: the American Falls on the left, Bridal Veil Falls in the middle, and the U-shaped Horseshoe Falls on the right. I found it relaxing to watch the water from my queen-sized bed, and I felt excited to fall asleep at night knowing the view would be the first thing I'd see in the morning, without having to face any of the crowds outside. Unlike most other hotel stays I've experienced, the falls were so entrancing that I didn't turn on the TV once during my stay.  I didn't expect my room to have a Juliet balcony with a door I could open to hear the water crashing down. The author photographs Niagara Falls Joey Hadden/Business Insider According to the hotel's website , the Sheraton is the only hotel in Niagara Falls to offer this type of terrace, which has a glass door that opens up to the outside, though I couldn't actually step onto it. I didn't expect to hear the waterfalls from my hotel room. With the door open, they were surprisingly loud. Opening the door gave me a better glimpse of Niagara Falls. I found listening to the falls to be calming. It reminded me of the white noise audio I sometimes use to fall asleep, except smoother and more powerful. Usually, I put on a playlist to start my day, but at the Sheraton Fallsview, I hopped out of bed and opened the door so I could get ready to the sounds of the crashing water. After the sun went down, I had no idea the falls would glow in a colorful light show. Joey Hadden/Business Insider While the falls are breathtaking during the day, staying in this hotel room made me think they may be even more beautiful at night . After the sun went down, I looked out the window to find the falls glowing in changing colors, courtesy of the Niagara Falls Illumination Board.  According to Niagara Parks , the falls glow every night of the year, and the changing colors represent sunrises, the aurora borealis, rainbows, and sunsets. I had no idea the falls would glow in color at night like this before visiting, so if I hadn't stayed in a  hotel with a view , I might never have seen them. Each night at the Sheraton Fallsview, I pulled a chair up to the window to watch the show. At 10 p.m., I watched a fireworks show explode over the glowing waterfalls without having to deal with the crowds. Joey Hadden/Business Insider I also didn't realize my room would give me a front-row view of a nightly fireworks show. During my first night in the hotel, after I was already mesmerized by the light show, I was completely awestruck when fireworks started popping off above the falls. The fireworks display happens every night at 10 p.m. from late May to early October, according to Niagara Falls Live . The show went on for about six minutes each night. I thought it felt magical.  Seeing the fireworks show from my bed was a happy surprise, and I was glad to avoid the crowds of people rushing to admire them from the same viewpoints below. I felt like a VIP on my own private perch and thought it made the nightly $500 price worth it. Read the original article on Business Insider
