events.title: Indian executives are gaining clout in US corporate boardrooms
events.summary: The share of Indian men among directors at Fortune 500 and S&P 500 companies has tripled since 2018, outpacing increases for women, black and Hispanic directors. After decades of climbing the executive ranks at US companies, more men of Indian descent are now entering the boardroom. A record 16 Indian men joined S&P 500 boards in 2026, taking directorships at companies including Walmart, Southwest Airlines and Western Digital, according to ISS-Corporate and data provider Equilar. Only white men and women added more seats. The surge caps a longer shift. The share of Indian men among directors at Fortune 500 and S&P 500 companies has tripled since 2018, outpacing increases for women, black and Hispanic directors, according to data from James Drury Partners. The boardroom gains come as companies put increased emphasis on directors with chief executive or operating experience – credentials that many Indian business leaders have accumulated after decades in the US, according to recruiters and the executives themselves. Of the 184 Indian men on Fortune 500 and S&P 500 boards, 77% have operating, or so-called profit-and-loss, backgrounds, the James Drury data shows. Roughly two-thirds have held CEO roles. That same pattern is evident among 2026’s directors, where two-thirds are current or former CEOs. They include top executives at Stryker and Linde, and the recently retired CEO of Albertsons. The gains come as companies pull back from diversity, equity and inclusion efforts. Even so, boards are continuing to change, with Indian men making particularly rapid inroads. Indian men now lead roughly a dozen blue-chip companies, including Alphabet , Microsoft and Procter & Gamble, underscoring their growing presence in the highest ranks of corporate America. Indian women, like women more broadly, have not seen the same progress in recent years, in part because they are less likely to have served as CEOs. There are notable exceptions. Former PepsiCo CEO Indra K. Nooyi and former Gap CEO Sonia Syngal joined the boards of Honeywell International and Tractor Supply, respectively, in 2026. Anand Eswaran, CEO of Veeam Software, was added to the board of technology company F5 in April. For Eswaran, 53, who came to the US more than three decades ago from India, each generation of Indian executives is building on gains made by earlier groups of workers who arrived after immigration rules were relaxed in the 1960s. To get to America, the aspiring executives had to compete with millions of their countrymen for spots at the best schools, Eswaran said. They advanced from entry-level jobs to operational roles as they proved their mettle. The first big company CEOs in the late 1990s opened up opportunities that have been widening ever since, he said. “Those are massive filters,” Eswaran said. “You get people who are sort of comfortable with risk and probably pretty hard to rattle.” One of the early pioneers was Raj Gupta, who in 1999 was appointed CEO of a Fortune 500 company when he took over speciality chemical maker Rohm and Haas. He was only the third CEO of Indian heritage in the Fortune 500 at that time. His career includes work on 15 public boards, including HP and DuPont de Nemours, and seven private boards. Gupta said his first board stint came at a speciality gas company in Philadelphia when he was still among the candidates to become CEO of Rohm and Haas. His boss at the time said it would be valuable experience for his eventual promotion. Now 80, Gupta said his board service years are done and he is currently teaching future business leaders at Wharton and Harvard. Gupta said early mentors helped him transition from employee to leader, advising him, for example, to speak up more in meetings rather than save his best ideas for private conversations. “The mindset was, if I continue to perform well relative to my peers, I’ll be recognised and I’ll be promoted,” he said. “But I think the recognition of understanding was that your softer skills, influencer skills, listening ability, after you reach a certain level, are more important.” The career trajectory of many of today’s Indian business leaders is similar to that of Rakesh Sachdev. He started in the US as a senior engineer at auto supplier Cummins in 1981 before rising to become chief financial officer and later president of Asia-Pacific at Arvin Meritor. During the financial crisis in 2008 he left the auto industry for biotech company Sigma-Aldrich, where he rose from CFO to CEO in 2010 and later sold the company before taking another CEO role. He is currently the chair of paint maker Axalta Coating Systems, which plans to merge with Dutch paint company Akzo Nobel later in 2026. He says he will be the chair of the new company. Sachdev, 70, said he has helped recruit Indian executives to boards and increasingly sees them included on slates of potential directors for boards on which he serves.

events.title: Hafary’s founding family offers 64 cents a share to take company private
events.summary: The offer values Hafary’s 430.55 million issued shares at about $275.6 million. Hafary's founding family, through 23 Capital, has made a cash offer of 64 cents per share to take the company private, with nearly 90% of shares already committed. The offer values Hafary at about $275.6 million and aims to delist the company from SGX, citing low trading volume and no need for future equity capital. Privatisation will save listing costs, provide management flexibility, and allow shareholders to exit at a premium without brokerage fees, with a formal offer expected soon. SINGAPORE – The founding family of local tile supplier Hafary Holdings has launched a cash offer to take the company private, with shareholders holding nearly 90% of its shares already committed to accepting the bid. The voluntary conditional offer of 64 cents a share is being made by 23 Capital, a company owned by Hafary chief executive Low Kok Ann and his children, Low See Ching and Audrey Low Bee Lan, according to an exchange filing on Sept 28. The price is 4.9% above Hafary’s last traded price of 61 cents on Sept 25, and 19.9% above its volume-weighted average price over the preceding 12 months. Unless a competing offer emerges, the price is final, said 23 Capital. Its offer values Hafary’s 430.55 million issued shares at about $275.6 million. Hafary’s three family members, who together hold 39.14% of Hafary, have undertaken to accept the offer. Hap Seng Investment Holdings, which holds a further 50.82%, has also given an irrevocable undertaking. Their combined holdings amount to 89.96% of Hafary’s shares. The offer is conditional on 23 Capital receiving enough acceptances to exercise its right to compulsorily acquire the remaining shares, after which 23 Capital intends to make Hafary a wholly owned subsidiary and delist it from the Singapore Exchange. It said it would not take steps to restore the company’s public float if it falls below the required 10%. Citing Hafary’s low share trading volume as one reason for the offer, 23 Capital added that the move gives shareholders an opportunity to exit at a premium without paying brokerage fees. Hafary has not raised equity capital through the stock market in the past 10 years and is unlikely to need access to it in the foreseeable future. A privatisation would also save listing costs and give management greater flexibility, it said. A formal offer document is expected to be sent to shareholders within 14 to 21 days of the announcement, after which the offer will remain open for at least 28 days. Hafary began in 1980 as a ceramic tile shop in Balestier, co-founded by Low Kok Ann. It has since expanded into stone, mosaics, wood flooring and bathroom fittings, supplying home owners as well as designers, contractors and property developers. The holding company listed on SGX’s Catalist board in December 2009 and moved to the mainboard in June 2013.

events.title: Strategic allocation to Asia fixed income
events.summary: Strong regional fundamentals make Asia an attractive diversification option for fixed-income investors, with Hong Kong dollar bonds playing a distinct role [The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.] Global markets currently face high levels of uncertainty. Inflation remains elevated in developed economies, the trajectory of monetary policy is unclear, and complex geopolitical tensions add further complexity to the outlook. At times like this, it makes sense for fixed-income investors to broaden their portfolio exposure. Asian fixed income presents attractive opportunities to diversify across markets, supported by solid macroeconomic fundamentals, accelerating AI development, ongoing supply chain realignment and relatively compelling yields. Its strength compared to other regions makes a strong case for investors to consider a strategic allocation to Asia within their global portfolios. It is a challenging time for the global economy. Not only are there serious disruptions to trade, but there are also growing concerns about the high levels of indebtedness in some of the largest economies. But despite this difficult backdrop, Asia remains an economic bright spot, accounting for around 60 per cent of global growth,¹ while at the same time presenting relatively benign levels of inflation compared to many Western economies. Asia is not homogeneous. Each market presents its own growth story, monetary policy trajectory and credit profile, creating a diverse set of opportunities for strategic and tactical allocations that can potentially result in a more resilient portfolio. Hong Kong dollar (HKD) bonds can complement a broader Asia allocation. For investors with HK dollar liabilities, the market provides high-quality assets in the currency of the obligation. For US dollar-based investors, Hong Kong’s link to the currency can also help limit risk. Issuers in the Hong Kong dollar market typically have good credit quality, including the Hong Kong government, as well as other well-rated quasi-sovereign, supranational and corporate issuers. Yields in Hong Kong are relatively modest, but the market’s robust credit fundamentals and relatively contained local inflation have supported its defensive characteristics. This can make HKD bonds a comparatively stable source of defensive exposure. For some investors, accessing the market through individual securities can be challenging. Institutional minimum sizes can put many issues out of reach, liquidity can be thin in some parts of the market, and most HKD non-government bonds are issued through private placements rather than via public offerings. For that reason, many investors find a fund or exchange-traded fund the more practical route into the asset class. Asia US dollar credit: resilience amid volatility Beyond local currency markets, the Asia US dollar bond market can provide diversification benefits for global investors, underpinned by robust investment-grade fundamentals and improving high-yield conditions. Asia dollar investment-grade credit has historically held up well in periods when external events have widened spreads – such as the Covid-19 pandemic, the start of the conflict in Ukraine in 2022, the implementation of new tariffs by the US in 2025 and the energy price shock that followed the blocking of the Strait of Hormuz off Iran. Resilience, in part, reflects the quality and composition of the Asia credit universe. About 87 per cent of the constituents in the J.P. Morgan Asia Credit Index are classified as investment grade.² Furthermore, the index’s composition has become less concentrated over time, with greater diversification across geographies and sectors. Within Asia credit, two investment themes stand out. The first is supply chain realignment. Many international companies are implementing so-called “China plus one” strategies, which extend supply chains to other Asian economies. At the same time, more mainland Chinese companies are expanding manufacturing operations across the region, especially in Southeast Asia. All this drives capex and local infrastructure financing, which may support a broader regional corporate bond universe – potentially giving investors greater diversification and more opportunities to identify relative value across markets and sectors. The second theme is artificial intelligence (AI). Select Asian technology companies are likely to see demand lift as AI adoption widens. Momentum remains strong in Asian hardware tech, including leading regional foundry and memory chip companies, which stand to benefit from data centre demand and a memory super-upcycle. Fundamentals in these segments remain stable, with manageable capex well within financial limits. Often thought of as an equity story, AI is increasingly relevant to Asian fixed income as well, broadening the investable universe.

events.title: Stocks slip in Asia as oil climbs, bonds retreat
events.summary: Japan’s Nikkei gained 0.8%, while South Korean stocks dipped 0.6%. SYDNEY – Share markets were mostly lower on Sept 28 as oil prices popped higher again amid doubts the United States and Iran will reach a truce any time soon, keeping bonds under pressure ahead of a week packed with economic news. Over the weekend, US President Donald Trump rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, claiming Tehran was desperate to make a deal. Trump said talks would continue this week, though Iran shows no sign of watering down its proposals. Brent futures rose 2.1% to US$106.49 a barrel, bringing gains so far in September to almost 18%, while US crude futures added 1.5% to US$93.84 a barrel. A dearth of refining capacity has in turn lifted diesel prices to all-time highs far above crude, raising the risk that inflation will become embedded in pricing and wage decisions. Central banks have responded with a round of rate hikes, with the Reserve Bank of Australia likely to be the next to tighten when it meets on Sept 29. Markets now imply a 66% chance the US Federal Reserve will hike for a second straight meeting in October, with around 90 basis points of tightening priced out to late 2027. At the same time, a run of strong US economic data has supported expectations for corporate earnings even as bond yields surge, so underpinning equities. The Atlanta Fed’s GDPNow measure is forecasting growth of a racy 5% for this quarter. Activity has also proven upbeat in Asia and Europe, thanks in part to the boom in artificial intelligence investment. “The global expansion appears to have entered a phase of broad-based strength rarely seen over the past two decades,” said Bruce Kasman, chief economist at JPMorgan. “Amidst strong growth and firming perceptions of resilience to high energy prices, it is no surprise that rates are moving higher while equity prices remain close to record levels,” he added. “What is most notable about recent market moves is their extension of higher policy rates well beyond the coming year.” Japan’s Nikkei went flat, while the volatile South Korean stock market slid 2.4%. MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan eased 0.6%. Chinese blue chips slid 1.4%, and are down more than 5% for the month. On Wall Street, S&P 500 futures fell 0.3%, while Nasdaq futures shed 0.5%. In Europe, EUROSTOXX 50 futures firmed 0.4%, while DAX futures gained 0.3% and FTSE futures added 0.2%. Yields on 30-year Treasuries nudged up to 5.5185%, near their highest since 2004, having climbed 27 basis points just this month. Two-year yields have shot up 55 basis points in September in anticipation of Fed hikes. Mark Cabana, a rate strategist at Bank of America, sees further room for bonds to sell off as markets price higher Fed funds. “The repricing may not stop until there’s clear evidence that financial conditions have become sufficiently restrictive,” he warned. The spike in yields raises borrowing costs globally just as tech firms are borrowing billions to fund their AI expansion, while also lifting the discount applied to company earnings. The US data calendar is packed with readings on inflation, gross domestic product, manufacturing and jobs. The key September payrolls report on Oct 2 is forecast to show a gain of 85,000, while the unemployment rate is expected to hold at 4.1%, with some chance of a dip to 4%. The recent spate of upbeat figures has boosted the dollar index to two-month peaks at 101.39. The euro was down at US$1.1380, having lost 2% so far in September. The dollar edged up to 157.53 yen, after dipping on Sept 25 when Japan’s Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said Trump had voiced concerns about yen weakness. Sterling was just above three-month lows at US$1.3240, having been helped somewhat by hawkish comments on rates from Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey. In commodity markets, non-interest-bearing gold fell 1.7% to $4,212 an ounce, having fallen more than 4% in September as yields shot higher. REUTERS

events.title: Amazon evaluating drone deliveries in Australia, Asia
events.summary: E-commerce giant Amazon.com is preparing to launch drone deliveries in Australia and other nations. “As Prime Air evaluates Australia and other countries, we are hiring a Head of Regulatory Approvals, Australia – the person responsible for navigating Australia's aviation regulatory system and securing every approval required to deliver to Australian customers by drone,” reads a recently published job ad. Whoever gets the gig in Australia will report to someone who holds the title “Leader, Prime Air Expansion – Asia Pacific.” The Register asked Amazon to comment on the ad, and which other Asian countries it plans to enter. The company had not responded at the time of writing. Whoever gets the job “will be measured by the approvals you obtain, the timelines you hit, and – ultimately – Australian customers receiving drone deliveries.” That wording suggests Amazon intends to operate Prime Air in Australia and is doing rather more than market evaluations. In August, Amazon said it plans to operate Prime Air drones in “nearly” 500 cities and towns across the USA this year. Meta and Singapore sling scammers Meta last week announced that information-sharing with Singapore Police helped the social media giant to identify a new variety of attack and led it to take action against more than 113,000 entities and pages connected to fraud and scams on Facebook and Instagram. Meta calls the new scams calls “shell pages” and says they “look empty and harmless” because they don’t include ads or content that violates Zuck’s T&Cs. “But scammers had pre-built infrastructure, ready to be activated for scam campaigns at a moment’s notice,” Meta says. “Working from SPF’s signals, in July 2026, we took action against over 3.6 million shell pages before they could be used – and we’re now pursuing further disruptions against this type of scam.” “Rather than responding to individual reports, this collaboration focuses on proactive network disruption – where SPF information helps Meta’s investigators identify and dismantle entire ecosystems of bad actors,” the company asserted. Meta didn’t say how scammers could sign up for 3.6 million pages without it noticing. Nothing has a plan to conquer India’s consumer tech market Consumer electronics outfit Nothing, which has carved out a small niche with well-priced Android devices, has decided to spin out its Indian subsidiary CMF. CEO Carl Pei explained the move as a bet on India’s growing electronics manufacturing industry spurring demand for local consumer tech brands. “Every country that has manufactured consumer electronics at scale has eventually produced its own global champions. Japan did. Korea did. China did, and I watched it happen over the better part of a decade living there,” he wrote. “India is next. It's already the world's second largest smartphone manufacturer, with the largest youth population on earth and one of its deepest software talent pools. What it doesn't have yet is a global consumer electronics brand of its own. That will change. The only questions are when, and how.” Pei thinks the how is spinning out CMF, a Nothing sub-brand that makes budget-priced phones, audio kit, and smartwatches. Bangkok floods – brace for supply chain impact When heavy rains and subsequent floods struck Thailand’s capital city Bangkok in 2011, facilities operated by hard disk manufacturers Western Digital and Seagate experienced damage that disrupted production for months. Bangkok was again hit by rain and severe floods last weekend, but to date The Register can find no evidence of problems at major tech companies. Western Digital and Seagate have not announced any issues, while hyperscalers Google, Microsoft, and AWS also report their local infrastructure is operating normally. Thailand’s government announced a two-day holiday to help residents clean up after the flood, which saw much of Bangkok under 30 centimeters or more of water. India’s Economic Times reports that the companies offered over 150 jobs to IIT students, but didn’t make the appointments. events.title: Italy attracts wealthy Chinese property buyers with food, fashion – and flat tax
events.summary: Hong Kong and mainland investors are increasingly eyeing property in Italy, drawn by its lifestyle and flat tax regime, agents say Italy is becoming a magnet for wealthy property investors thanks to its high quality of life and flat tax regime, and interest is also on the rise among mainland Chinese and Hong Kong buyers, according to property agents. Rome introduced a flat tax regime nine years ago to attract high-net-worth individuals, with foreign residents allowed to make a flat annual tax payment of €300,000 (US$342,000) on all their overseas income under the scheme’s latest rules. events.title: AOC test-runs a Senate bid in upstate New York
events.summary: BUFFALO, N.Y. — Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez 's flirtation with a 2028 Senate bid is getting real — more real than the presidential buzz around her might suggest. She's barnstorming through upstate New York, meeting with local officials, and kicking off a voter turnout program that could help her collect valuable data for a possible Senate campaign. Why it matters: Whether the House member from New York runs for Senate or the White House is one of the biggest questions hanging over the 2028 Democratic presidential primary. Zoom in: Her swing through Buffalo and Ithaca was officially aimed at boosting Democratic turnout in the midterms. But it doubled as a way to test AOC's appeal far from her home base of Queens and the Bronx, and build relationships with locals. In Buffalo, she met privately with Mayor Sean Ryan, then held an impromptu press conference with him, generating coverage of the duo on local TV news. She and her team later kicked off a voter-turnout operation that could help them gather information about the electorate outside New York City. "I want to be very forthright about our intentions here, which is to transform the state of New York," Ocasio-Cortez told activists in a Buffalo arts center who were attending a training session of hers aimed at getting inactive voters to the polls. In Ithaca, she appeared at an apple festival with Rep. Josh Riley (D-N.Y.) and on Sunday was scheduled to headline a "Students vs. Billionaires" town hall. It's friendly terrain: The city is home to several democratic socialist elected officials, and Ocasio-Cortez is a member of the Democratic Socialists of America. The intrigue: AOC says she's genuinely undecided on whether to run for the White House or Senate. Her recent activities upstate suggested that wasn't a head fake. Ryan said Ocasio-Cortez has been talking with state officials about how help communities beyond New York City. Meanwhile, some influential Democrats in early presidential primary states have told us they haven't yet heard from AOC. And she hasn't made public visits this year to some of those early states, a contrast from other potential 2028 contenders who are practically living in them. Many political insiders believe that if Ocasio-Cortez were to run for an open Senate seat, she'd clear the Democratic field. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.), who's in his fifth term, hasn't said whether he'll run for reelection. AOC was greeted like a rock star on her upstate tour, with Ryan remarking that at City Hall "a young man really, literally shouted across the lobby, like, 'Oh my gosh, congresswoman, can I take a picture with you?'" Yes, but: Ocasio-Cortez also has taken several steps that could point toward a presidential run. She's toured the country, moderated her stance on some cultural issues, and opened up about her egg-freezing journey. She recently told the New York Times she'll consider whether to run for president after the midterms. Between the lines: One exchange with Ocasio-Cortez offered a window into how she is approaching her decision. We asked her how she's thinking about the future of the progressive movement as she weighs a White House run. In the last two open Democratic presidential primaries, there has been a clear progressive standard-bearer, and many on the left think she's their only hope for 2028. She didn't seem persuaded that by that argument. "The movement is so much bigger than any one person," she told us. The bottom line: AOC suggested that her choice won't be solely about ideology. "These decisions aren't always about punditry or ideology. It's about putting the country first," she said. "What's important is ending … the corrupt reign of the Trump administration, as well as any of its acolytes." Asked whether that means she's weighing "electability" as she determines her next move, she replied, "I don't see who wouldn't."

"I was just starting to decorate the walls and get things to a state where the space was me," they said. Jamie Bruce is still sleeping on a fold-out couch waiting for the house repairs to be finished. ( ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters ) "Then I watched my little dragons that were on the wall slowly disappear under the water." Floodwaters peaked at 186 gigalitres a day, leaving only concrete and wooden cladding behind in Jamie's bedroom. The family's staircase is being held up by two wooden panels. ( ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters ) Jamie's mum, Kay Bruce, describes the first 12 months following the flood as "a nightmare". The family spent five of those months living out of a friend's large tin shed. "Thinking about [that time] now still brings tears to my eyes," Ms Bruce said. Frustrated by the delay for their insurer to send out a tradie, the family took a payout so they could source their own workers. "[I had] so many phone calls where they would never come back to me," she said. Kay Bruce says the situation has taken a mental and physical toll on her family. ( ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters ) "I've got a spreadsheet, and it shows just name after name after name." Despite trying to project-manage the rebuild, after three years Ms Bruce was still yet to have a tradesperson follow through and do the job. "I can't understand when people make arrangements to come and do work or make quotes and then just don't turn up, don't phone you, don't text you," she said. Her husband, Rob Bruce, said that while the process had been exhausting for the whole family, it came with a level of guilt. "We have friends that lost their entire place and they're still in the caravan park whilst their houses are being built," Mr Bruce said. "We'd feel bad knowing that our place was all done and they're still in the caravan park waiting." With the cost of materials to build a home spiking in recent years, Mr Bruce said the family felt trepidation about the future. "It worries me that it's going to be a hit for us [to rebuild]," he said. The cost to build a new home in South Australia has risen by almost 40 per cent since 2021, according to the Insurance Council of Australia. It is something social policy, climate and international engagement manager Alix Pearce says is a growing national issue. "We're seeing this [rise] in materials and labour costs, too; for example, roof tiles have gone up 77 per cent over the last five years." Alix Pearce says governments need to increase investment in resilience to build stronger homes. ( ABC News: Greg Bigelow ) Ms Pearce said state and federal governments needed to do more to uplift their investment in housing resilience and address tradie shortages across the country. "We need to see increased investment in trades and construction, particularly in those high-risk areas in Australia." There is currently a 141,000-person skilled workers shortage nationally, according to Master Builders Australia. In South Australia, about 20,000 workers are required over the next five years to meet major project and housing demand, according to a state government spokesperson. The spokesperson said it has committed $11 million over the next two years, alongside the federal government, to help the travel expenses of rural or regional apprentices travelling long distances to keep them on the job. Master Builders Australia projects a worker shortage of 935,600 by 2035. ( ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters ) "The new measure will support an additional 400 regional apprentices and trainees to undertake their training," the statement said.

events.title: Walmart denies using personal info to set prices as it expands digital shelf labels
events.summary: Walmart is aiming to assuage customers' fears about its new pricing technology. NEW YORK -- Walmart is aiming to assuage customers' fears about its new pricing technology as it rolls out digital price labels at its stores. In a statement posted on the company's website, Walmart Inc.'s CEO John Furner vowed that the Bentonville, Arkansas-based retailer isn't using personal information like income, shopping history or a customer's willingness to pay to set prices, and it won't be doing so in the future either. “We don’t set different prices based on who you are or the time of day, and we won’t,” Furner wrote Friday. “Whether you’re buying groceries or electronics on a hot afternoon or in a sudden rush for an item, it’s never a reason to charge you more.” The pledge from Walmart comes as concerns are mounting from some shoppers, consumer advocates and lawmakers skeptical about the rollout of digital price labels by the discounter and other stores. Digital price labels are rapidly replacing paper shelf tags at U.S. supermarkets and let stores change prices instantly from a central computer instead of having workers swap out paper labels by hand. Furner noted that Walmart is also holding its artificial intelligence shopping assistant Sparky to the same promise and won't be using the bot to raise a customer's price or hide lower-priced options that meet their needs. Furner said such practices would violate the company's “every day low prices” business model. He also noted that prices can change: Walmart lowers them when it can pass savings along, or sometimes raises them because an item costs more to buy or to transport, he said. Walmart executives have repeatedly said it uses electronic shelf price tags to help the retailer change prices consistently and match what rings up at checkout. It also saves workers time and reduces labor costs by replacing paper tags. Last month, the Federal Trade Commission said that it's putting companies on notice that the practice of personalizing pricing could violate consumer protection laws. The agency said it does not have the legal authority to ban personalized pricing in all circumstances, but it issued a new bulletin that warned companies that they must disclose to customers how the personal information is being used to set a price. events.title: Mapping Biology’s Next Frontier
events.summary: BioMap co-founder and CEO Liu Wei believes the future of life sciences will be shaped not by artificial intelligence alone, but by the combination of foundation models, biological data and AI-native laboratories that can turn ambitious predictions into real-world discoveries. After two decades backing some of the world’s earliest artificial-intelligence companies, Liu Wei has moved from investor to builder. A longtime technology enthusiast, Wei spent 18 years as an early-stage investor, including as general partner of Legend Star Ventures and founding CEO of Baidu Ventures. He has invested in and incubated more than 400 early-stage technology companies worldwide, including more than 50 focused on AI for life sciences. Today, as co-founder and CEO of BioMap, he is betting that biology’s next transformation will come from combining foundation models, biological data and AI-native laboratory equipment. “We think big,” he says. “Our vision is to build a map – hence ‘BioMap’ – of the biological world. Whether you are studying a protein, cell or organ, you should be able to generate predictions and results.” Rather than selling point solutions that handle single tasks, BioMap aims to become a shared infrastructure layer for life sciences: a biological equivalent of Google Maps on which others can build drugs, tools and services. BioMap grew from a shift Wei identified as an AI investor: the data revolution had finally reached biology. “As an early-stage AI investor, we always looked for new sensors and sources of data,” he recalls. Over the past decade, high-throughput technologies such as single-cell omics, and proteomics (two innovative techniques for analysing the molecular components of individual cells) have driven an explosion of data across laboratories and pharmaceutical companies. Yet biological abundance has not made discovery simpler. Wei argues that biology’s search space is vastly larger than those of language, images or even the physical world. “The biological world is perhaps 1,000 times more complex than the physical world,” he says. “We aren’t just talking about individual proteins or cells. As you move from single cells up to complex organisms, the complexity multiplies massively at every step.” That makes data both the driver and the bottleneck. High-quality, task-specific validation data remains scarce and expensive, particularly when researchers are exploring something genuinely new. BioMap’s response is to build biological foundation models that can learn from heterogeneous, imperfect data while powering specialised applications. The firm has trained models on more than a million biological elements across evolutionary trees, including more than 20 billion different protein sequences, then layered hundreds of task-specific models on top. “Across over 300 task models, we have reduced the data required by an average of 90 per cent,” Wei says. “In many cases, we use only one-tenth of the data needed to train a task model from scratch.” This matters because, in discovery, the necessary data often does not yet exist. BioMap’s broad evolutionary foundation is intended to propose designs in sparsely explored regions, while directing scarce real-world laboratory experiments towards the most promising candidates. Wei also sees BioMap as a “linker” rather than a lone disruptor, connecting bioinformatics companies, modality-specific biotech start-ups, equipment makers, academic laboratories and major pharmaceutical groups. The aim is to get experimental data into models more efficiently. “There are many companies working on bioinformatics, drug modalities and laboratory equipment,” he says. “We want our ecosystem partners to join us in building something much bigger.” Looking five to 10 years ahead, Wei believes AI will change not only how drugs are discovered, but also which drugs are worth pursuing. “First-in-class research will become easier, less expensive and more likely to deliver strong returns,” he predicts. In the past, many biotech companies, particularly in China, defaulted to fast-follower or best-in-class strategies because first-in-class programmes were costly and failure-prone. Foundation models, Wei argues, can evaluate multiple constraints at the outset. “AI can predict and generate designs while considering several parameters at once,” he explains. “It is not limited to predicting a single property.” That means toxicity, manufacturability and yield can be assessed during design rather than discovered late in development, potentially improving the odds for genuinely new therapies. The same tools could support work in rare diseases and smaller patient groups. Large pharmaceutical companies often pursue broad, high-revenue indications, even when distinct patient subgroups respond differently. “Companies may know that different subgroups respond differently, but the economics often favour developing a single drug for one large market,” Wei says. “Not every group receives the same benefit.

events.title: SA's statewide blackout was 10 years ago — but electricity debate is still live
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Energy Minister Tom Koutsantonis inspected damaged towers near Melrose in the aftermath of the blackout. ( ABC News: Dean Faulkner ) Blackouts come in different forms — there are those that affect memory, and those that affect electricity. But no mental blank has impaired the vividness of Tom Koutsantonis's recollection of the time when, on a tempestuous spring afternoon 10 years ago, power was cut to the whole of South Australia. Reflecting on the precise moment when the statewide blackout began, the Labor MP smiled wryly at the irony of the circumstances in which he found himself at the time. "I was actually in the parliament on my feet moving legislation relating to the National Electricity Market (NEM)," he said recently. About 4pm on September 28, 2016, electricity supply to more than 850,000 properties and approximately 1.7 million residents was disrupted, leaving South Australia in darkness. Police directing traffic around Adelaide's CBD during the blackout a decade ago. ( AAP: David Mariuz ) Mr Koutsantonis was then the state's minister for energy — a portfolio which, despite changes of government in the intervening years, he holds again today. His first inkling that something was wrong was prompted by an apparent malfunction at the entrance to the parliamentary chamber. The billionaire bet that created the first big battery For former SA premier Jay Weatherill, the tweets that triggered the Tesla giant battery project created an opportunity — but also a shock. Suspecting there had been "some sort of brownout", he was then told by an advisor that what had occurred was far worse than that. In the same moment that Mr Koutsantonis heard parliament's doors start to glitch, energy industry analyst Danny Price was on his computer monitoring the situation closely. "I just saw demand drop off a cliff, so I knew straightaway it was a blackout," he said. "I wasn't surprised — I was watching the weather in South Australia for a day or two beforehand. You could see a very big storm was brewing." While supply was slowly restored over the coming hours, some parts of the state were without power for more than two days . A map from the time of the blackout showing outages across South Australia. ( SA Power Networks ) An early estimate of the economic impact concluded that the blackout cost businesses more than $360 million — but money wasn't everything . At Flinders Medical Centre, there were distressing consequences for prospective parents when dozens of embryos were lost at a private fertility clinic because mains supply was cut. At different times, energy policy, renewables and extreme weather have each been lambasted as the prime culprit for the statewide blackout. In a 2017 report, the Australian Energy Market Operator (AEMO) concluded that overly sensitive protection mechanisms in some of the state's wind farms were to blame . "Activation of this protection feature resulted in a significant sustained power reduction for these wind farms," the report stated. A lone policeman directs traffic near Victoria Square during the 2016 blackout. ( ABC News: Tony Hill ) AEMO found that the sudden dip in output triggered a power surge along the Heywood Interconnector from Victoria, which in turn caused the system to trip and SA to become "islanded" from the rest of the NEM. "AEMO cannot rule out the possibility that later events could have caused a black system, but is not aware of any system damage that would have done this." But the causes that were most immediately obvious on the day itself were the tornadoes, with estimated wind speeds of between 190 and 260 km/h, that ripped through SA's mid north , damaging critical infrastructure. A collapsed transmission tower near Melrose during a severe storm at the time. ( ABC News: Dean Faulkner ) Indeed, the most enduring imagery from the blackout is probably that of giant transmission towers lying collapsed and contorted in fields . "Two towers had been taken down by a freak tornado or hurricane," Mr Koutsantonis said. "Any time you take out transmission lines … you're going to have a shock to the system. "That caused a sudden loss of power and the system reacted according to the laws of physics." Energy economist Danny Price says renewables need the support of thermal generation. ( ABC News ) Mr Price also pointed to the weather — but said there was a failure of preparation at market level ahead of a "one-in-50-year storm". "[There were not] any gas generators running, which is crazy to me," he said.

events.title: Amodei critics target Trump with hit piece before White House dinner
events.summary: Opponents of Anthropic's Dario Amodei are circulating a highly negative brief about him to the White House ahead of an important dinner with President Trump , per an Axios review of the document. Why it matters: No company wants to be on Trump's bad side — and a Sunday night dinner between the president and Amodei could be what thaws relations after a year of tension. Behind the scenes: The brief, which is not an internal White House document, casts Amodei as having "a long record of attacking Trump" and having "deep Democratic ties." It notes the company's falling out earlier this year with the Pentagon as a "clear example of Dario showing he doesn't trust President Trump." The brief is intended for Trump's eyes and is likely to get in front of him, according to a source familiar with the internal workings of the White House. Its origin is unclear. It even reads in "Trump Talk," a name the president gives to his style of posting: "Dario claimed that AI would eliminate half of all entry-level white collar jobs as soon as this year. WRONG!" Between the lines: The brief's creators are appealing to a president who prizes loyalty and puts a premium on praise. Amodei's failure to communicate properly with the Trump administration has previously cost the company . Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Yes, but: Trump has also been laser-focused on winning the AI race and Anthropic is one of the few companies on the frontier of the technology. Anthropic is also valued at hundreds of billions of dollars and has plans to go public soon, making it even harder for the White House to ignore. "The WH is trying to get everyone seated at the table," one source told Axios. The bottom line: Anthropic and the White House both have something to gain from Sunday night's dinner, so long as Amodei's critics don't get there first. Marc Caputo contributed to this story

events.title: Banks cut rewards programs, free travel insurance amid surcharge ban
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Rewards programs and insurance perks in firing line after changes to bank surcharging rules Sweeping changes across payment systems will start on October 1. ( ABC Radio Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton ) After four decades as a Commonwealth Bank customer, Trevor Vienet is changing banks. That is because CBA has changed its association with the Qantas Frequent Flyer program ahead of the credit and debit surcharge ban announced by the Reserve Bank of Australia. It is the lesser-known side effect of the changes that begin on October 1 because banks' revenue will drop as they reduce the amount they charge businesses to bank with them. The Commonwealth Bank has introduced a new in-house rewards system called Yello, which Mr Vienet is not eligible for. "The [CBA] letter was, I'd call it a Dear John letter. It's like: 'You've had a long relationship, but it's all over,'" he said. After decades with the Commonwealth Bank, Trevor Viénet is moving much of his banking elsewhere. ( ABC News: Matthew Holmes ) From Thursday, businesses will be banned from adding a surcharge to customers using electronic terminals to pay for goods on card networks including eftpos, Mastercard and Visa. The cap on interchange fees paid by Australian businesses to banks for processing credit card fees will reduce from 0.8 per cent to 0.3 per cent, meaning businesses will pay lower fees but bank revenues will take a hit. In preparation for these changes, the major Australian banks are increasing credit card fees, reducing reward program perks and cutting back on travel insurance inclusions. "I was pretty angry … I've been a customer for 40 years, have held several accounts and three mortgages and paid those off," Mr Vienet said. The surcharge ban is expected to save consumers about $1.6 billion and businesses $200 million in surcharge fees annually. The changes to interchange fees — the fees banks charge businesses for using their systems — are estimated to reduce transaction fees from businesses to banks by about $910 million each year. Sally Tindall is the data insights director at Canstar. ( ABC News: John Gunn ) Canstar's data insights director, Sally Tindall, said it was clear the banks were not willing to wear the reduction in interchange fees. "They're looking to recoup at least some of that loss … the consumer, in many cases, will end up paying for part of this ban at the minimum, but also small businesses." But Australian Banking Association (ABA) chief executive Simon Birmingham said the changes implemented by the banks were expected. "That was one of the things that the Reserve Bank called out as not only expecting to see, but basically wanting to see," he said. Do you know more, or are you affected? Tell us here . Small businesses say prices may rise The almost one in six businesses that surcharge have until October 1 to make the necessary changes, and some are worried. Swim school owner Greg Hodge is working with his customers to change the way they pay for lessons, from credit card payments to bank transactions. Greg Hodge says the ban on surcharges will force him to increase the cost of swimming lessons. ( ABC News: Maren Preuss ) But if they can not switch to bank transfers, Mr Hodge may have to charge extra for each lesson to cover all banking costs. He is not alone. Australian Restaurant and Cafe Association chief executive Wes Lambert said many businesses were considering their options. "Many have indicated that they are going to increase their prices," he said. "Many have [also] told us they are going to stop taking certain credit card types [and] many have said that they're going to go to cash only." Despite the additional charging that may happen, the RBA's head of payments policy, Ellis Connolly, said he did not expect increases would have an "ongoing effect on inflation". Ellis Connolly says the surcharging changes will not have an ongoing effect on inflation. ( ABC News: John Gunn ) "In the end, the consumer was paying it either way, whether it was paid in a surcharge or whether it was paid in the end price," he said. While some businesses may be forced to increase the prices of goods and services, others have argued it is not that simple. Central Coast councillor Jared Wright said for a council to increase fees, it had to go through a "multi-month process" involving public consultation. He estimated the impact of the surcharge ban on his council, which is one of the largest in New South Wales, would be about $400,000 in lost fees, and was concerned about the possible flow-on effect to his constituents.

events.title: 'Something we've never seen before': The risk of AI bioweapons
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts How concerning is the biological weapon threat from AI systems? AI tools raise the risk that someone could develop a biological weapon. ( Supplied: Geralt/Pixabay ) The AI industry is suddenly rife with existential fears, with senior figures claiming it could "kill us all" within a decade. Dario Amodei, CEO of one of the world's largest AI companies, Anthropic, has called for a "slowdown" of AI development to prevent it outrunning our control. One particular fear is that AI could develop a dangerous biological agent, or a bioweapon. At the same time, biologists are showing AI can help them with useful research — including those employed at Anthropic, who have just announced AI has helped them discover a new class of enzymes they claim "could represent a new gene editing mechanism ". So is AI a biological threat, or a boon? It may be an uneasy mixture of both. Why does AI raise the danger of bioweapons? Labs around the world have had the tools to make dangerous biological agents, like viruses, for decades. But few people have known how to use those tools, and all of them are scientists who have spent years building their qualifications and credibility. Brendan Walker-Munro, a security researcher at Southern Cross University, says AI changes this. David Heslop, a public health researcher at the University of New South Wales, says the speed of AI progress makes him "very concerned". "The tools are advancing at a rate which means that human oversight is becoming challenging," Dr Heslop says. AI is moving at a pace that makes it hard for traditional biosecurity to keep up. ( Unsplash: João Pessoa ) An advanced AI model could give a user outside traditional systems the information required to make a bioweapon. "It could be a virus or it could be a bacteria, it could be a fungus, it could be something we've never seen before." Anthropic researcher says AI 'could kill us all' A researcher for AI developer Anthropic has quit the company and is calling on the industry to slow down. Equally dangerously, in Dr Heslop's opinion, an AI tool like a large language model (LLM) could help a bad actor plan to deploy dangerous material, including pre-existing viruses or toxins. Such work would still need a level of expertise and tens of thousands of dollars of lab equipment. "We're not at the point, yet, where the LLM gives you a superpower," Dr Heslop says. "But it's certainly something that could be done in a laboratory." AI could also be used to attack broader public health systems, like hospital infrastructure. David Kainer, a computational biologist at the University of Queensland, says the same tools applied to plant science could "potentially destroy large amounts of food production". "You could imagine something similar happening to engineer super-pathogens for crops." What sorts of biological threats has AI enabled? There are several cases where AI has already been used to help design dangerous biological agents. In 2022, researchers at the Collaborations Pharmaceuticals company showed they could use their company's AI software to make dangerous toxins . The company's AI tool was used to screen out drug candidates with high predicted toxicity. But the team found they could instruct it to do the opposite, designing new toxins in a matter of hours. Reporting rogue AI won't be enough to keep Australia safe, expert warns Controversial Sydney data centre project pulled amid community anger Get rules in place to hold data centres to account, experts tell Tasmania Migration cuts, AI and rising interest rates mean an era of long-term disinflation In its recent threat intelligence report , Anthropic highlighted five examples of people using its products "in ways that could support biological weapons development". Anthropic's models were used to do things like draft grant applications and analyse data in research that made human viruses more contagious, and venoms and toxins more deadly. All of these users, according to Anthropic, were "working scientists" outside the US using unauthorised software to gain access to the US versions of their products. Anthropic banned the users for violating supported region policies. Are there legitimate reasons for using AI? Biologists have used AI for positive purposes. AI program Alphafold, for instance, has been used to predict the shape of proteins for medicinal research, winning its creators the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. More recently, US researchers used generative AI to design new bacteria-infecting viruses that could become treatments against infection.

events.title: The Guardian view on Thames Water: Andy Burnham should nationalise this failed monopoly | Editorial
events.summary: The Guardian view on Thames Water: Andy Burnham should nationalise this failed monopoly Bill payers should not fund another rescue for financiers of the water industry. Public ownership can end the cycle of extraction and failure T his month, a cross-party parliamentary committee said Thames Water should be placed in temporary state control and that any takeover by its creditors should be halted. The MPs were right. The “ special administration ” regime keeps the taps running while shareholders are wiped out, creditors take a haircut and the firm’s £19bn of debt is restructured. But it must not then be handed back to private hands. After Thames Water has failed its 16 million customers, polluted rivers , paid out billions to shareholders and repeatedly demanded higher bills, a City-friendly reprieve would only reward the outrageous behaviour that the regulatory system is meant to deter. Ministers ought to seize the opportunity to nationalise Thames Water. In July, Andy Burnham agreed. On the campaign trail in Makerfield, he told reporters that “there’s a very strong case for public ownership [for Thames Water] to sort out its problems”. Having entered parliament and become prime minister, Mr Burnham is instead looking at letting elected mayors “ oversee ” private water companies. There is nothing wrong with more democratic scrutiny. However, oversight without ownership and proper control seems like a sleight of hand. Voices from different wings of the party recognise this. Mr Burnham can’t kick the decision down the road for ever. In less than two weeks, water privatisation will be on the ballot in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, when voters elect an MP to succeed Sir Keir Starmer. A campaign to boycott Thames Water bills has sprung up in the London constituency after repeated flooding caused by broken pipes. When asked by the Camden New Journal when the mains were last inspected, maintained or replaced, Thames Water gave “no answers”. If Labour cannot take a failing private monopoly that ruins lives into public ownership, voters may ask themselves who will? Polls suggest comfortable majorities of Britons believe water companies should be run in the public sector. Under Sir Keir, Labour’s review of the water sector ruled out nationalisation. Some claim that new models of corporate governance could “subordinate” profits to the common good . But it’s hard to see how a failed regulatory regime will be fixed by more regulation. History has been turned on its head when British Rail is cited as proof that nationalisation is wrong. The state-owned rail firm had productive staff working in an ageing railway starved of investment. By 2011, privatised rail cost 20%-30% more . Sound familiar? Mr Burnham called water “an industry where the shareholders never lose and the bill payers never win ”. Deeds, not just words, are needed. England and Wales are outliers : 90% of the globe keeps water in public hands because others understand that a natural monopoly in water offers no competition to raise standards and leaves households as captive customers for financiers eyeing easy profits. Nationalisation comes with a price tag. But, as the Institute for Fiscal Studies acknowledges, assessing the true cost to the state requires valuing the whole deal and future cashflows , not just looking at metrics that exclude most of what is being acquired. An efficient nationalised water industry should mean cheaper bills. Currently, Ofwat allows industry’s backers to recoup £22bn over five years. A Greenwich University study calculates that nationalisation could save households up to £160 a year by accessing low-cost state financing. The upshot of public ownership is that it puts an asset on the nation’s books, whereas privatisation puts the cost on customers’ bills.

events.title: The Guardian view on Manchester City: a strange kind of glory | Editorial
events.summary: The Guardian view on Manchester City: a strange kind of glory If a guilty verdict on multiple counts of financial misreporting is upheld against the club, its achievements in the modern era will be forever tainted I n surveys ranking the Premier League’s greatest moments, football supporters regularly give pride of place to Sergio Agüero’s championship-winning goal for Manchester City in 2012. Scored in injury time on the last day of the season, Agüero’s strike against Queens Park Rangers delivered the first league title for City since the 1960s. Knocking their historic rivals Manchester United into second place, it also signalled a new era in which the club replaced United as the dominant force in the English game. “Aguerooooooo!” – the incredulous single-word response from the match commentator Martin Tyler – has entered football folklore. But an asterisk may now be needed at the end of all those Os. Reports that an independent panel has found Manchester City guilty of breaking Premier League rules between 2009 and 2023 cast a dark shadow over that day, and much else besides. During that period, the club won seven Premier League titles, six League Cups, three FA Cups and the Uefa Champions League, all while under the ownership of Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, a member of the Abu Dhabi ruling family. The inescapable implication of the apparent ruling is that those trophies were won unfairly. The guilty verdict on more than one hundred separate charges against City has yet to be officially confirmed. It may be assumed that the club – which has consistently denied wrongdoing – will launch an appeal. But rivals are already taking advice over compensation claims and the Premier League, which began its investigation in 2018 after whistleblower leaks, must contemplate how tough it wants to be on the most successful English football club of the current era. If the verdict is upheld, the punishment should be exemplary and severe, given the threat to the integrity and credibility of the world’s most popular domestic football league. In essence, Sheikh Mansour and his board stand accused of illicitly bankrolling the City men’s team’s ascent from Premier League also-rans to repeat champions, using inflated sponsorship deals and off the books payments to fuel the rise. The club hierarchy’s aggressive response to scrutiny conveyed a sense that it seemingly thought extreme wealth – and the political heft of Abu Dhabi’s soft-power project – could confer a kind of impunity. The Premier League’s investigators should be congratulated for staying the course, and this extraordinarily long-running saga should now be brought to as swift a conclusion as possible. It is hard not to feel some sympathy for Manchester City supporters, confronted with the likelihood that the greatest period in their club’s history will be forever tainted. On the pitch, City’s football during the Abu Dhabi era has at times been of a sublime quality, overseen by an inspired coach in Pep Guardiola. But off it, the biggest financial scandal in English football history is a reminder that the volume of money now washing about at the top of the game has been bad for its sporting soul. During the Premier League boom years, great footballing institutions have lost their spiritual bearings as dubious billionaires , debt-leveraging carpetbaggers and petrostates have muscled in for a piece of the action. In the case of Manchester City, the Sheikh Mansour takeover delivered undreamt of success and that Agüero moment. But if it took persistent cheating to get there, it was a worthless kind of glory. events.title: Most of UK’s essential food supply grown in drought-risk areas, report warns
events.summary: Keys crops such as cereals, potatoes, sugar and oils grown in areas with moderate to very high risk The vast majority of the UK’s essential foods, including cereals, potatoes, sugar and oil, are grown in areas of England rated as having a moderate to very high risk of drought. A very high proportion – 81% – of England’s fresh produce is concentrated in parts of the country that are already experiencing water stress, according to the analysis by the nature-focused investment fund Rebalance Earth . Three-quarters of England’s wheat (77%), barley (75%) and oilseed rape (74%) grow in parts of the country rated as being at a moderate to very high drought risk, along with 70% of sugar beet and 67% of potatoes, it found. It said about a quarter of the country’s staple crops were grown in areas facing an acute risk of drought, including 30% of wheat and barley, 28% of oilseed rape, 27% of fresh produce and 21% of potatoes. “Drought builds slowly and quietly, and rarely gets the same attention as flooding, but its impact runs right through the economy: lower yields, strained supply chains and higher prices in all of our shopping baskets,” said Kirsty Wilman, the fund’s chief operating and financial officer. Some of England’s traditionally most productive agricultural areas – such as East Anglia, long known as the country’s breadbasket, and Kent, often described as the garden of England – are among those facing the greatest pressure from drought and have seen prolonged periods of dry weather in recent years. The yield from this year’s cereals harvest in England and Wales was described as disappointing in the final 2026 harvest report from the Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board (AHDB), with volumes of wheat, spring barley and oats below historical averages across the UK. Crop yields are also significantly lower than normal on the Elveden estate in Suffolk, which is owned by the Guinness family and includes 9,000 hectares (22,000 acres) of farmed land. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning “For three years out of five we have been in drought conditions,” said Andrew Blenkiron, who manages the farms on the estate in Breckland, an area on the Suffolk-Norfolk border known for its sandy soil. One of England’s largest commercial farms, they grow cereals including wheat and barley and root crops including onions and potatoes. “Water for food is key for us to function as a business and make sure we produce 100,000 tonnes of food here on an annual basis,” he added. Despite the challenges, Blenkiron believes the UK needs to better use its water resources to continue growing staple foods in productive areas. “If we didn’t grow on this land that is totally suitable for it, we would just import more and let other people deplete their natural resources.”

events.title: Trump: 5 terrorism suspects in U.K. base incident were under investigation
events.summary: British police arrested five men Sunday on suspicion of terrorism near a U.K. air base used for U.S. operations in Iran , as President Trump said the suspects had been under investigation. The latest: "Working with Britain, it was an amazing job," Trump told reporters Sunday morning. "We had them under investigation. They were looking to do big damage to our fort, and working with the British worked out great and we got them." The big picture: Officials declared a major incident and set up roadblocks overnight near RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, southwestern England. The incident, which British investigators did not immediately link to Tehran , comes one day after Trump said he'd rejected the latest Iranian proposal to end the war — though he told Axios's Barak Ravid on Sunday that he expects fresh talks this week. State of play: Police received a call around 12.45 a.m. Sunday local time relating to "three suspicious vehicles" that appeared to be traveling towards the air base used by the U.S. 501st Combat Support Wing and the 420th Air Base Squadron, per a Metropolitan Police statement . Armed officers responded in the area of Whelford, a village some 33 miles from the city of Oxford. There they arrested the men "on suspicion of committing offenses under the Explosives Act" and they were further arrested "on suspicion of preparation of a terrorist act, contrary to section 5 of the Terrorism Act," according to the statement. Zoom in: U.K. counter-terrorism official Vicki Evans said officers established a 400-meter cordon (roughly a quarter-mile) around vehicles in the area while the British Army's Explosive Ordnance Disposal unit conducted examinations. "As a precaution, around 85 households have been evacuated whilst these examinations take place," she said in a statement. A nearby leisure centre was opened for people evacuated from the area. Context: RAF Fairford is the U.S. Air Force's preferred bomber forward operating location in Europe and supports a variety of missions and exercises throughout the year, according to the Air Force. Flashback: Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps warned in July that any base used for attacks on Iranian territory would be considered a "legitimate target" in a statement that specifically referenced U.S. B-1 bombers flying from RAF Fairford. What they're saying: The 501st Combat Support Wing told Axios that no U.S. Air Force personnel were involved in the incident. "The 501st Combat Support Wing appreciates the swift response and continued support of our local law enforcement partners," the statement said. "We remain in close coordination with our UK partners to help ensure the safety and security of both our military and local communities." events.title: Armani's business and creative evolution on show in Milan a year after founder's death
events.summary: Giorgio Armani’s empire is taking shape a year after the designer’s death MILAN -- The future of Giorgio Armani ’s empire is coming into sharper focus a year after the designer’s death. On the runway in Milan, his signature elegance defined the latest collection previewed on Sunday, while behind the scenes talks are set to begin on the sale of a stake, as stipulated in his will. Armani gave preference to LVMH, L’Oréal and EssilorLuxottica as potential buyers of a 15% stake to be sold within 18 months of his death on Sept. 4, 2025, at the age of 91. Chief Executive Giuseppe Marsocci told reporters backstage at the runway show that there were no favorites and that the stake could potentially be split among all three companies. “It is not written in stone that there has to be one,” he said. Marsocci said the will allowed discussions to begin only after the first anniversary of Armani’s death but declined to confirm whether they had started. “The assumption” that talks were underway “may have some logic,” he said. The recent appointment of Dario Vitale as head of accessories at Giorgio Armani and creative director of Emporio Armani has generated interest in the fashion house’s creative future. No date has been announced for his runway debut. Asked whether Vitale’s role could expand, Marsocci said everything was evolving. “From here into the future, you never know,” he said. Lean, fluid trousers and long dresses shaped the silhouette, often paired with rigid bodices. The collection was titled “Evolution.” “It evolved in the sense that it is fashion that everyone can wear,” said Silvana Armani, the late designer’s niece and longtime head of womenswear. She departed from her uncle’s legacy in one important way: incorporating cotton, a textile that she said he didn’t like but which she “adores.” The designer’s presence was most felt in the collection in two pieces: a recreation of the formal double-breasted Communion suit that Armani wore when he was 8-years-old and a graphic jacket bearing his smiling image. events.title: Turkey's ruling-party deputy chair steps down after share trading allegations
events.summary: Turkey’s ruling party has accepted the resignation of its deputy chairwoman ISTANBUL -- Turkey’s ruling party accepted the resignation of a deputy chair on Sunday after she was accused of selling shares worth tens of millions of dollars shortly before a stock market crisis. Turkish stocks plunged Sept. 16 amid suspected share-price manipulation involving several investment funds. Fatma Betul Sayan Kaya, deputy chairwoman of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan ’s Justice and Development Party, or AKP, requested to be relieved of her duties on Saturday. AKP spokesman Omer Celik said Erdogan had accepted Kaya's resignation. “We declare that all those who are involved in irregularities, corruption, abuse or anything that causes harm will be held accountable,” Celik added. IRGC will target US ships in Indian Ocean if fighting resumes, official says District attorney reopens case of alleged Cornell University 'gang rape' White House orders over $800M in funds rescinded Zeynel Emre, a spokesperson for the main opposition New Party, claimed that Kaya, who served as Turkey 's family and social affairs minister from 2016 to 2018, received some 1.3 billion Turkish lira ($27.5 million) when she sold shares shortly before the stock market plunged. Emre said Kaya had bought the shares, most of them in shipbuilding company Ozata Denizcilik, for 63.4 million lira ($1.3 million) in April. Kaya, who served as Turkey ’s family and social affairs minister from 2016 to 2018, has not responded directly to the allegations. events.title: After nixing Iran proposal, Trump tells Axios he expects talks this week
events.summary: One day after he rejected an Iranian proposal to end the war, President Trump told Axios in a phone interview on Sunday that he expects U.S. negotiators to engage in more talks with the country this week. Why it matters: Qatar and other regional mediators are trying to revive negotiations between the U.S. and Iran, but the two sides are far apart on the key issues. While Iran wants to focus any talks on the Strait of Hormuz and the U.S. naval blockade, the Trump administration is demanding that Iran agree to nuclear concessions. Two regional sources confirmed Trump's comment about more talks this week. They said they expect another round of indirect dialogue between the U.S. and Iran as early as Monday. But it isn't clear if the gaps can be bridged. What he's saying: "I expect more talks with Iran [this week]. They want to make a deal, but it is not the deal that I want to make. It is what we would have maybe agreed to a year ago. They overplayed their hand," Trump said. Asked if he is considering resuming strikes against Iran, Trump said: "I am always thinking about it." State of play: In the meantime, Trump said, the U.S. military is facilitating a lot of oil out of the Strait of Hormuz. He said that over the weekend the largest amount of oil transited through the strait since the war began. "More than 20 million barrels," Trump said. A U.S. defense official confirmed Trump's assertion, saying that on Friday night 22 million barrels of oil were exported through the strait. Driving the news: U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner held a new round of indirect negotiations with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York last Tuesday. Qatari officials participated, passing messages between the two sides. Araghchi delivered to Witkoff and Kushner Iran's conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz and resuming nuclear talks. Iran proposed reopening the strait and restarting nuclear talks in a week, if the U.S. lifts its naval blockade, removes sanctions on oil sales and reinstates a ceasefire across the region. Trump rejected the Iranian proposal on Saturday. Behind the scenes: But a U.S. official and two regional sources told Axios that Qatari mediators are continuing shuttle diplomacy to try to reach a deal. On Thursday, the prime minister of Qatar met in New York with the Iranian president and discussed the potential deal with the Trump administration. Shortly after, senior Qatari officials met Witkoff and briefed him. A regional source with knowledge of the indirect negotiations said the Qatari mediators discussed the original Iranian proposal with both parties and provided a compromise proposal to both sides to review. What to watch: Over the weekend, the Qatari mediators have been going back and forth separately with Iranian and U.S. negotiators on changes to the text. Qatari mediators are expected to meet separately with Araghchi and Witkoff as early as Monday. The other side: Araghchi told NBC on Sunday that despite Trump's rejection of the Iranian proposal, Iran still wants a diplomatic solution. He said that the midterm elections aren't part of Iran's calculations. "We only care about our national interests. We are ready for negotiations," he said. "Although we heard from President Trump that he's rejecting this deal ... we are still waiting for an official response through the mediators," Araghchi added.
